A potentially devastating cyberattack on individuals and organizations can occur through a sophisticated yet incredibly simple attack technique known as a Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attack. This type of attack, facilitated by a malicious entity positioning themselves between the user and a trusted network, allows them to intercept and manipulate communication while masquerading as the genuine intermediary. In the context of machine learning-based systems, an adversary can exploit this vulnerability to manipulate users into submitting model inputs that have been tampered with, ultimately leading to inaccurate predictions and potentially severe consequences. In this research, we delve into the efficacy of machine learning classifiers when subjected to MitM attacks, identifying vulnerabilities in their design that allow adversaries to manipulate users into submitting compromised inputs. Through our analysis, we demonstrate how an adversary can utilize generative models to produce manipulated inputs, and propose a novel metric to measure a system's resilience to such attacks. Utilizing DNN and CNN models as examples, we showcase the significant impact an MitM attack can have, and highlight the advantages of adversarial training as a potential countermeasure to mitigate this type of threat. Additionally, we investigate the potential for deep learning models to learn from training data that has been manipulated by an adversary, which we term the Man-in-the-Middle-in-the-Training phase (MitMitrP). Our findings reveal that certain neural network architectures can adapt to such a threat, and propose the use of adversarial training with multiple generators to mitigate both MitM and MitMitrP threats. With our research, a significant understanding of the internal workings of machine learning classifiers is gained, and potential countermeasures to safeguard against such cyberattacks are introduced. Our code is publicly available on GitHub for reproduction and future validation. Additionally, a virtual machine containing our research data is hosted on Testbed.cvc.nist.gov for public access. Our research follows the ethical guidelines outlined in the IEEE Computer Society's Ethics Board Policy and was approved by the NIST Institutional Review Board. This study utilized a dataset of proton-proton collisions that took place at a 13 TeV energy at the LHC, accumulating a total of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity. Data analysis was performed by comparing it to various models of dark matter and top quark pair production, setting limits on cross-section at 70-118 fb, 0.35-1.21 fb, and 0.99-3.76 fb for the $t$ plus $D$meson, $t$+$t\bar{t}$ with invisible particles, and $t$+$t\bar{t}$+$D$meson processes respectively, under different assumptions at the 95% confidence level. Furthermore, a study of top quark and $D$meson pairs revealed a cross-section range of 0.05-0.44 fb, also at the 95% confidence level. These storms exhibit significant intensity fluctuations in very short time frames and are typically associated with intense microwave burst activity. To study the dynamic properties of these storm sources, we analyze noise storm observations in combination with magnetic field data from the Sun's surface. By using the SDO/AIA's high-resolution imaging capabilities and the Helioseismic and Magnetic Sun Observatory's (HMI) vector magnetometry, we identify complex structures in active regions undergoing rapid changes. These observations indicate the rapid conversion of energy between the Poynting vector and electric field. Furthermore, we find that the cross-polarization area element of the magnetoflux tube is linked to the frequency and energy of the storm. These findings mark the first discovery of a link between solar noise storm characteristics and magnetic field dynamics, and we propose that similar processes in other active regions may also give rise to type-I noise storm activity. Additionally, we suggest that the dynamic changes in the noise storm source may be passed on to the storm itself, causing it to evolve and express the changes observed in the storm source's parameters. These ideas imply that the stimulation of noise storm activity is closely tied to the dynamic movement of magnetic field flux in the Sun's photosphere and atmosphere. By identifying a connection between these two phenomena, we may achieve a deeper understanding of the independent and spontaneous development of solar activity. The analysis also reveals that the temporal sequence of these storm source parameter changes is consistent across multiple noise storm cases. These changes often begin with a small increase in the magnetic field's strength, followed by an increase in the cross-polarization area element and finally, the frequency and energy of the storm. The analysis further reveals that the frequency of the storm is directly linked to the 5-minute oscillations of the storm source's magnetic field. These oscillations may also be passed on to the noise storm, causing its frequency to shift. The noise storm activity is found to be more pronounced in areas with 5-minute oscillations that are oriented in a specific direction. Conversely, we find that the noise storm activity is less prominent in areas with 5-minute oscillations aligned in a different direction. These oscillations may also be responsible for the noise storm activity being concentrated in specific areas. By studying this radiation, we can examine the atom's internal dynamics and identify its energy states. This architecture comprises an generative adversarial network that produces restored images, as well as a self-encoding network extracting text features from the input, both working in tandem. Our model leverages multiple loss functions to optimize restortion quality, text extraction, and the alignment of restored images with true labels. We evaluate the efficacy of our model on the datasets "17SDR", "MetRGS", and "NWDT", demonstrating its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods across various evaluation metrics. When the user inputs their ID card number, the system detects and matches the user's information with the digital representation to verify authenticity.  This verification process was integrated into an existing Java-based application.  This new feature enables automatic verification of ID cards by scanning the card and validating the extracted information with the one stored in the database.  The verification process involves OCR, extraction of information, and finally a comparison with the digital representation to confirm authenticity. The proposed system was designed using a modular approach with the OCR analysis layer being the most critical layer. IEEE 802.11p is a wireless standard widely utilized in Vehicle-to-Vehicle (V2V) communications. As it does not utilize traditional Fixed Channel Assignment (FCA), it dynamically selects channels from the 5.9 GHz frequency band based on the IEEE 802.11p Dynamic Channel Assessment (DCA) algorithm. This approach, while capable of optimizing channel selection, is susceptible to interference and cannot guarantee the optimal transmission of data. To address these limitations, a novel Temporal Averaging based Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model is proposed in this study for enhanced IEEE 802.11p DCA performance. This proposed framework combines the capabilities of LSTM, a type of gate-based neural network, with time averaging to make more informed channel selection. Additionally, the researchers offer a numerical analysis of various channel occupancy models and suggest an adaptive strategy for grid search optimization within the IEEE 802.11p DCA algorithm. This proposed Temporal Averaging LSTM model is shown to successfully mitigate interference and achieve improved performance in IEEE 802.11p Vehicle-to-Vehicle communications. This is corroborated by the simulation results, which demonstrate that the model maintains high data transmission rates (above 90%) while minimizing the false alarm rate to less than 5%. To validate the efficacy of this approach, the researchers analyzed various Channel Path Gain (CPG) models, including the Alpha-Kappa model, and proposed an optimized grid search algorithm for the IEEE 802.11p DCA. This was achieved by numerically analyzing the CPG models and identifying the optimal channel selection strategy. To facilitate real-world implementation, the proposed Temporal Averaging LSTM model is shown to be compatible with the IEEE 802.11p standard and could be integrated into the DCA algorithm using its In-Building Map (IBM) and Neighbor Discovery Process (NDP) components. This is illustrated by the model's successful operation in a simulation scenario, where it successfully selected the highest-quality channel and maintained a low interference rate. To conclude, the proposed Temporal Averaging LSTM model offers a capable solution for enhanced IEEE 802.11p DCA performance, achieving improved data transmission rates and reduced interference through optimized channel selection. Our work focuses on constructing a scalable cognitive architecture that can facilitate large-scale multi-agent collaborative learning between human and robots. We introduce a new approach that combines multi-agent reinforcement learning with a distributed neural network to model other agents. This architecture is applied in a large-scale network of autonomous robots that learn from each other to achieve common goals in complex environments. The effectiveness of this architecture is demonstrated through a comparison of two methods: one that models other agents through a neural network and another that uses a neural network to directly learn from the interactions with those agents. Our results show that agent models are not necessary for successful collaboration and that the indirect experience through multi-agent interactions is sufficient for achieving good performance. Our findings have significant implications for the design of open and scalable cognitive architectures that can support large-scale collaborative learning between human and robots. The mean absolute deviation (MAD) from the median is a measure of dispersion commonly used in applications such as investment analysis and financial modeling. Unlike traditional measures of dispersion such as variance and interquartile range, MAD has a major draw-back: it is a biased estimator. In this study, we present a novel, high-precision approach for eliminating bias in the MAD estimator. Biased-correct MAD (BC-MAD) is assembled as an linear combination of n-1th power mean and the interquartile range, both of which are well-defined for any law of large numbers convergence. We demonstrate that BC-MAD converges linearly to the true MAD as n increases without bound, thus achieving the same convergence rate as the classical MAD estimator. Our results are further validated by simulations demonstrating high efficiency in the estimation process. Additionally, simulations reveal that BC-MAD exhibits superior robustness in the presence of outliers compared to alternative estimators such as the modified MAD (M-MAD) and the modified biased-correct MAD (m-BC-MAD) proposed in this study. The task of relation extraction aims to extract relevant information from natural language texts, specifically by identifying relationships between entities mentioned within these texts. Traditional methods for relation extraction often rely on classification models that associate entities with pre-defined relationship categories. However, these models struggle to handle entities that are not part of any established relationship, leading to subpar performance in cases where few contextual clues are available to support a clear association. Recent advancements in pre-trained language models have improved the overall effectiveness of relation extraction pipelines, but have yet to effectively address this entity-relationship ambiguity. In response, this study proposes an innovative approach that utilizes knowledge graph link prediction to enhance the modeling of entities and their associated relationships. By integrating this technique into a state-of-the-art BERT-based relation extraction model, we demonstrate improved accuracy in multiple datasets and an increased ability to correctly identify relationships involving ambiguous entities. Our methods demonstrate consistent performance across various evaluation metrics, including F1-score, mean rank, and mean squared error, as well as in scenarios involving different knowledge graph embeddings and knowledge graph completion methods. Specifically, our results show a 6.3% improvement in F1-score for the SBLEX dataset and a 5.9% improvement in mean rank for the TAC KBP dataset, along with significant reductions in mean squared error for both datasets. These outstanding performance metrics underscore the value of leveraging knowledge graph link prediction in the context of relation extraction. Our code repository is publicly accessible at https://github.com/asharif/PGNE. geometric and algebraic techniques. By examining p-norm based neural networks, 
we investigate the geometry of their loss functions and analyze the behavior 
of optimization algorithms. This analysis is based on a simple yet powerful 
identification method that allows us to map the loss functions to a more tangible 
geometry. By using this geometric framework, we can gain a deeper understanding 
of why certain models and optimization techniques excel, and also identify new 
models and algorithms with promising prospects. Ultimately, this study aims to 
provide a comprehensive and unified view of the deep learning landscape.

A common challenge in simulating hubbard models using neural networks lies in handling the sign problem that arises due to the complex weight values of the network. This paper explores the incorporation of complex-valued weights into neural networks with a focus on circumventing the associated sign issue. It examines various initialization methods for complex weights and proposes a new measurement to gauge the phase ambiguity of these weights. Furthermore, the study investigates the impact of rotating and scaling the weights to mitigate the sign problem. Experimental results obtained from simulating a 2D hubbard model with a 10x10 lattice structure, demonstrate that neural networks with complex weights can accurately predict the model's ground-state energy at finite temperatures, without being confined to the restricted manfold of real weights. This finding holds true even in cases where the system exhibits significant sign alternation in the real part of the wave function. Additionally, the study finds that networks with complex weights tend to exhibit improved correlation between the network's and the target ground-state energies at higher temperature values compared to real-weight networks. Consequently, the study suggests that neural networks with complex weights can be effectively utilized to predict thermodynamic properties of hubbard models at finite temperatures, without being limited by the constraints of the restricted real-manifold. Code for the paper is publicly available on the github repository: https://github.com/zhenghangao/hubbard_neural_network.git. In particular, the code contains functions for intiailizing complex weights, defining the ground-state energy estimator, and testing the network at finite temperatures, which are specifically designed for the wavefunction-based neural network (wfbnn) method. This work is expected to extend the application of neural networks to simulate hubbard models to higher temperature conditions, thereby enabling a broader range of thermodynamic property predictions. Related theories and experiments on the wavefuction-based neural network (wfbnn) method have been presented in hangao's phd thesis and other research papers, which are also publicly available on the arxiv platform. Recent studies have uncovered serious flaws in the design of adversarial robust deep learning models, revealing that certain samples can illicitly manipulate labels from artificial models. This has prompted a revised goal: achieving verifiable adversarial robustness, where claims of robustness are supported by verifiable guarantees. Unfortunately, current methods for implementing verifiable adversarial robustness are limited to simple linear models, while more complex models such as generalized linear regression and neural networks cannot be handled. This work seeks to close this gap by introducing an innovative approach for estimating the robust Bayesian posterior distribution in scenarios where the design of adversarial samples is also considered. We model sample generation as a complex computer program and employ a refined reinforcement learning strategy to solve the resulting mixed-integer convex program, often within a reasonable timeframe. This approach is paired with a parametric Markov chain Monte Carlo method for drawing random samples from the robust Bayesian posterior, while also providing a verified upper bound on its entropy. Experimental findings have demonstrated that our approach can accurately estimate Bayesian posteriors in high-dimensional settings and achieve the smallest known upper bounds on entropy and log-likelihood in models with nonconvex constraints. The integration of verifiable adversarial robustness into Bayesian inference has been made possible by our approach, allowing for the robust identification of predictive distributions and regions of support. The efficacy of this inference method has been demonstrated in various verification and machine learning challenges. All of our code, including mathematical formulations, algorithms, and numerical examples, can be accessed via the verinfer Python package. This package offers a verifiable adversarial robust version of scikit-learn and PyTorch Bayesian modules, while also providing a verifiable version of the torch package. A novel prediction method, known as ProCS, has been developed to accurately estimate the chemical shift of amide proton atoms in proteins, allowing for the identification of distorted regions in protein structures. This prediction method, which integrates quantum mechanical and empirical techniques, has been demonstrated to have an correlation coefficient of approximately 0.80 between predicted and experimental values for a large protein dataset. ProCS has been successfully used to verify and refine the structure of G-segment, a hyper-stable protein found in the HLA-A2 matrix of the human MHC I family. Preliminary results have shown that ProCS can help minimize irregularities in protein structures, suggesting its potential as a valuable tool for refining protein structures. Additionally, ProCS's ability to predict chemical shifts for large proteins, such as antigens and toxins, makes it a valuable tool for investigations in immunology and the design of therapeutic antibodies. This method has the potential to contribute significantly to biochemistry and structural biology. All existing and proposed code used in this research is publicly accessible on the GitHub platform at https://github.com/WhittensteinCorporation/procs. Furthermore, the ProCS web server, which offers a range of functionality for the analysis and refinement of protein structures, is available at https://procs.whittenstein.com. This includes the ability to upload and refine PDB files using the ProCS method. Quantum-mechanical-derived parameters for amino acid residues and various ionizing agents, which are essential for the operation of ProCS, are also publicly available on the GitHub platform at https://github.com/WhittensteinCorporation/procs_parameters. These parameters, known as'resc', significantly contribute to the speed and efficiency of ProCS predictions, allowing the method to handle large proteins and be used for the analysis of protein structures in an independent and self-contained environment. This means that ProCS can be used to refine protein structures on standard laptops and desktops, making it a valuable tool for a wide range of research applications in structural biology. It has the potential to significantly expand the scope of protein structure refinement, particularly for difficult cases such as large proteins, protein complexes, and enzymes. These challenging systems have been in need of a more efficient and precise refinement method like ProCS to better understand their functions and design new drugs. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it impractical to conduct exhaustive experiments to determine the optimal loss function for a specific task. Furthermore, the overfitting of a model in response to increased training data is another common issue. To investigate these concerns, we conducted a comprehensive study examining the impact of loss function variation in deep learning classification tasks. Our experiments involved evaluating the performance of twelve commonly used loss functions across six datasets, while also analyzing the effect of increased training data and the influence of model size. Our results indicate that no single loss function surpasses the others in terms of performance across all evaluated datasets. However, the optimal loss function often depends on the specific dataset and task. Moreover, our experiments revealed that more complex datasets and larger models require robust loss functions with the capacity to adapt and generalize. Our findings also show that overfitting in large models can be mitigated through the use of regularization techniques and early stopping. Ultimately, our study's findings underscore the need to select an appropriate loss function in accordance with the specific requirements of a given task. Our code repository can be accessed at https://github.com/asharakeh/loss-functions-experiments. Our report detailing all experimental results can be found in Appendix D.

In the context of perturbation theory, a particular decomposition of the graph functions into a sum of connected, yet interacting regions is referred to as parquet decomposition. Historically, achieving this decomposition has been a significant challenge within various perturbation theories; however, the development of modern symbolic-physical methods has made it feasible to obtain the parquet decomposition in multiple contexts. We explore the application of the Hamiltonian viewpoint in obtaining the parquet decomposition within the frameworks of functional Bethe-Sommerfeld equations and functional Bethe equations. It is demonstrated that both frameworks naturally yield the parquet decomposition through the resolution of a certain integral equation. Additionally, we find that the Hamiltonian viewpoint offers valuable insights into understanding the structure of X-ray scattering spectra and the correlation functions of system observables. We verify these results in the specific cases of certain fermionic and bosonic systems by analyzing the eigenvalue problems derived from the Hamiltonian viewpoint. We show that the resolved integral equations result in disconnected solutions, which correspond to distinct eigenvalue problems, and that the solutions to these problems directly correspond to the parquet decomposition components. We further emphasize that the proposed method can be extended to contend with systems that exhibit charge nematic order. We then apply the Hamiltonian viewpoint to derive expressions for various system properties, including the density of states and the structure function. Our approach is then validated by comparing its results to those obtained using the state-of-the-art full spectrum real-time dependent quantum Monte Carlo method. The comparison shows that the Hamiltonian viewpoint accurately predicts both the position and the width of the quasiparticle peak in the density of states. Moreover, we find that this approach accurately predicts the peak value and the width within approximately two orders of magnitude. We further note that while the peak value is outside the convergence range we used, the predicted width matches the quantum Monte Carlo results within the convergence range we used. Furthermore, we observe that the predicted structure function values are in line with the findings from the state-of-the-art full spectrum real-time dependent quantum Monte Carlo method for energies up to approximately one third of the band width. We note that the upper energy limit we used is representative of typical experimental x-ray scattering spectroscopy capabilities. We verify the accuracy of the predicted structure function by examining not only the absolute values but also the patterns of oscillation as a function of momentum. We emphasize that the symbolic physical method we used allows for the calculation of system spectra in systems that are beyond the reach of perturbation theory, which represents a significant advancement in this field. We propose a new form of engaged learning where the learner and teacher compete in a strategic game. The learner aims to minimize uncertainty about the teacher's action by first selecting a strategy through exploration, and then the teacher responds by choosing the action that will most disrupt the learner's decision-making. Unlike the optimistic assumption in typical engaged learning, our model considers a skeptical teacher who seeks to mislead the learner. As a result, the learner must adopt a cautious approach to learning. Building upon this game-theoretic framework, we derive general strategies for both the learner and teacher in both finite and infinite exploration settings. Additionally, we prove that a specific strategy that combines exploration with aggression achieves the optimal level of performance in the infinite setting. The maximin strategy, which is the highest level of performance that the learner can achieve when assuming the worst-case scenario, is also established. The maximin value, which represents the performance when the learner is most cautious, is derived for both the regret and excess risk metrics. Moreover, we demonstrate that various general strategies, including the pre-post experiment design, do not achieve the maximin strategy, and suggest a new 'double-aggressive' strategy that performs better. The theories and algorithms we've developed are further illustrated using simulation experiments. The maximin strategy we've developed is also proven to be adaptable to settings with additional constraints, including the scenarios in which the teacher's action has varying degrees of impact. The learner must also learn to adapt to unknown variance in the teacher's action, which presents an additional challenge. The optimality of a specific strategy, which is a variation of the double-aggressive strategy, is also proven when the learner is able to estimate the teacher's action disturbance variance. The algorithms we've developed are further illustrated using real-world experiments involving imitation learning. To study the time-dependent nature of musical complexity, we applied
information theory to analysis of sound waves from recordings of the top 200
charts in the US from 1960 to 2009. We calculated the average number of bits
required to describe the acoustic features of music in periods of five years each.

Our results show that musical complexity increased steadily over the nearly
five-decade study period, with fluctuations averaging 0.5 bits per year. The
rate of complexity growth slowed significantly after 1980, and fluctuations
became much less regular. We also found that the patterns of changes in the
sizes of sound wave features within music, specifically the frequencies and
amplitudes, contributed about equally to the overall increase in complexity.

To determine if this trend is unique to Western music, we applied the same
analysis to traditional African music recorded in the 1970s, finding that
musical complexity is indeed lower in African music by about 3.5 bits. We were
unable to detect any decrease in complexity over time within the African
data, and our results suggest that the differences in complexity between Western
and African music are largely due to the types of patterns within the sound
waves, rather than the patterns of how those sounds are arranged. We confirm
that our results are robust to variations in how the data is represented using
symbols, and that the patterns of changes in musical complexity are highly
correlated with the opinions of music experts. Finally, our study provides
further evidence that musical complexity is an important property that can be
quantified, and that it is closely related to the information carried by
music. We show that our measure of complexity is highly correlated with the
amount of information carried by music, and that this correlation holds not
just within our data, but also when comparing our results to a different
dataset. Overall, our study provides a quantitative understanding of how
musical complexity has changed over time, and how it relates to the inherent
properties of sound waves. We found that musical complexity increased
significantly over the nearly five-decade study period, and that the patterns
of changes in complexity are highly correlated with the opinions of music
experts. We were also able to apply our theoretical framework to analyze
complexity in other areas, and our results suggest that the patterns of
changes in complexity may be more constrained and predictable than previously
appreciated. Furthermore, our study demonstrates that musical complexity is
an information-theoretic property

In ideal two-dimensional fluids with the presence of surface hinges, a specific type of topological structure known as angular vortex loops emerges, which is characterized by their 2D winding number. This study demonstrates that these vortex loops possess several key properties: they are isolated from each other due to their finite size, the surface hinges localize the vorticity within a specific area, and the vorticity's overall 2D integral is zero. Moreover, we establish that the 2D vorticity field is governed by a specific Helmholtz equation centered at the hinge's location. This equation's solution is shown to be fully determined by the value of the vorticity at any point on the hinge. This finding implies that the properties of the vortex loops are entirely defined by the hinge's geometry. This result is reminiscent of the theory of helical structures in three-dimensional fluids. Finally, we provide a practical example of a simple flow profile that incorporates multiple connected angular vortex loops. This scenario illustrates how multiple isolated vortex loops can connect to form more complex configurations. Additionally, we observe that the solution of the Biot-Savart law at any point in the fluid is proportional to the local curvature of the hinge at that point, which suggests the existence of specific flow profiles depending on the hinge's curvature. This connection remains an unsolved problem and offers an exciting area of research exploration in this field. This study provides a fundamental understanding of the properties of angular vortex loops and lays the groundwork for future studies on ideal two-dimensional fluid dynamics. Additionally, we propose several future research directions. These ideas originate from the intriguing relationships and patterns we have identified, which we believe can lead to significant advancements in this area. Specifically, we suggest investigating specific flow profiles based on geometric criteria and studying the linking properties of the vortex links. These research avenues are relatively self-contained and can be developed with relative ease. On the other hand, we also pose more challenging questions, such as generalizing our results to semi-deterministic fluid models and exploring the asymptotic behavior of the vortex loops as they collapse. These problems are more complex and demanding, but addressing them could lead to breakthroughs in these research areas. Overall, this study aims to contribute to the ongoing research on ideal two-dimensional fluid dynamics and highlight new and exciting research possibilities. The connections between this subject and TQFT, as well as the inherent geometric properties of the vortex loops, offer promising avenues for future investigation. The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) is a causal parameter that can be estimated in two steps: first, predicting the likelihood of treatment and control given certain characteristics with a model, and then using those predictions in a second step to weight observations for a reliable estimate of the ATE.  In the first step, nonparametric and parametric methods have been explored, with notable successes using machine learning approaches to model the treatment decision in the target population.  However, the second step, weighting observations, has been less explored.  Despite the many possibilities, two methods - the Standardized Inverse Probability Weighting (SIPW) and the Generalized Weighted Average (GWA) - have been the focus of recent research, with the former relying on a model of the outcome to standardize weights and the latter relying on a model of the treatment decision to predict the probability of treatment and control.  Both methods have been successful estimators of the ATE, but have some notable limitations.  In particular, the SIPW estimator relies on a model of the outcome to perform well, while the GWA estimator relies on a perfect model of the treatment decision, though it is robust to misspecification in that sense.  Building on this research, a new method has been developed that shares characteristics with the GWA estimator, but has been modified to address the potential for bias in the SIPW estimator when the model of the treatment decision is misspecified.  The resulting method has been standardized, and can be estimated using machine learning techniques to model the treatment decision in a relaxed manner.  When the model of the treatment decision is correct, this method reduces to the GWA estimator, while also performing similarly to the SIPW estimator when the model of the treatment decision is correct.  Key features of this method include its ability to be estimated with a machine learning model that treats standardization as a classification problem, along with an intuitive interpretation that can be utilized in future studies as a testing ground for the validity of the model.  The method has been implemented using a specific neural network that treats the treatment decision as a multi-class problem, along with an evaluation of its performance using simulated data.  When compared to the GWA estimator, this method has been found to be a viable alternative, though it has been noted that the choice of network architecture is a delicate task.  Furthermore, the method has been observed to be more robust to the choice of network architecture than the SIPW estimator, while also performing well in the presence of misspecification.

In Offline Reinforcement Learning, we construct representation learning strategies called offline view selection methods to develop representations that can withstand data corruption. Unlike existing approaches that focus on optimizing a single offline RL objective, we aim to create a family of representations that remains robust to various levels of corruption. To achieve this, we introduce a new objective for view selection that combines both a traditional offline RL objective and a measurement of the selected views' similarity to uncorrupted datasets, solving it through a series of regularized reinforcement learning problems. We then show that in certain scenarios, this method allows for nearly full control of the selected views and can recover representations that are close to those in a dataset that has not been corrupted, even if it has been partially corrupted. To demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, we test it on a simple simulation and find that it permits recovery of parts of the state action space even when a significant proportion of the dataset has been corrupted. The idea behind our method, which we call Corrup RL, can be applied to many different problems and we believe it has the potential for significant practical impact. To illustrate this, we also test Corrup RL on a simple driving simulation and find that it enables recovery of the state-action visited distribution, including the position of the vehicle. Details of our code can be found on this GitHub repository: https://github.com/ashwink/Corruption-Resilient-Offline-RL. This work is inspired by our earlier research on representation learning in RL, which we carried out during our time at Cornell University's ML Research Group. The current research has significant applications in areas such as autonomous driving and robotic surgery, where corruptions can take the form of sudden changes in environment, such as traffic signal changes or medical procedure interruptions. In these domains, the ability to recover representations that are akin to those in a healthy or nominal state could be particularly valuable. In modern research on data-driven systems, a primary focus lies on overcoming challenges presented by high-dimensional complexities, sensitivity to noise, and limited availability of data. A powerful tool for addressing these challenges is the dynamic mode decomposition (DMD), yet its effectiveness is hampered by two major limitations. Firstly, it is incapable of handling non-linear systems, forcing researchers to linearize the dynamics in order to apply it. Secondly, it is extremely sensitive to noise, which further limits its practical use. In order to overcome these limitations, a novel kernel-based approach is proposed, utilizing optimization techniques to learn a suitable kernel for each specific system. This new method, known as the linear and non-linear clarification optimization (LANDO) method, is capable of accurately capturing the dynamics of both linear and non-linear systems, while also resisting noise and generalizing well to unseen data even when obtained from a limited dataset. A comprehensive series of numerical experiments, conducted on diverse systems of varying dimensions, confirms the exceptional performance of the proposed LANDO method. Additionally, the authors provide explicit mathematical proofs of several key aspects of the method, including its ability to learn a suitable kernel for non-linear systems and its generalization performance. A software package, available for public download, enables users to easily apply the proposed LANDO method to their own data, regardless of its format or origin. In particular, the package includes a range of pre-computed kernels, allowing users to easily utilize the LANDO method by simply substituting the provided kernels into the algorithm. These kernels have been pre-computed using diverse techniques and are guaranteed to be accurate, including: a) a low-rank kernel, derived from the existing DMD method and subsequently optimized; b) a Stein kernel, known for its ability to efficiently learn a suitable kernel; c) a Charlier kernel, part of a general family of potential kernels which can be efficiently learned. These options, combined with the extensive evidence of the method's performance, facilitate the use of the LANDO method in a variety of applications, such as modeling solar radio burst dynamics or capturing non-linear patterns in climate systems. In these applications and many more, the LANDO method emerges as the first choice for dimensionality reduction, regression, and forecasting. In a particular analysis, the authors apply the LANDO method to solar radio burst data, using a Charlier kernel to model the non-linear dynamics and subsequently achieve a 97\% accuracy in forecasting bursts on a given day. These results, and many more, demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed LANDO

Our findings suggest that rapid spikes in core energy are caused by the combined effect of reduced mass and core contraction, resulting in the core's entropy decreasing in the long term. We observe a correlation between the minimum core mass and the pulse period of white dwarfs, which follows a linear pattern, and predict that the spin velocity of these stars will eventually stabilize at a certain threshold. Furthermore, a specific technique was formulated to identify symmetries in Lagrangian dynamics of any order, which simplifies the derivation process. Additionally, this method was successfully applied to a few theoretical and experimental phenomena that were previously considered challenging, including the motion of a particle in a wave field and a spinning top on a surface. A comprehensive list of Noether symmetries in various physical systems has been compiled and made available in an online public table. Three-dimensional model retrieval techniques are typically based on the analysis of existing three-dimensional models. In this research, we take a distinct approach and focus on using three-dimensional drawings as input to retrieve suitable three-dimensional models from a database. To achieve this, we first developed two novel methods to create three-dimensional representations from virtual reality-based 3D drawings captured through VR drawing. The converted models are then compared to real 3D models using a point cloud comparison metric. Following these developments, we conducted two user studies to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed methods. The first study compared the performance of the two methods in model retrieval, considering the impact of drawing style and representation. The second investigation focused on assessing the accuracy of the converted models and drew parallels between the effectiveness of the converted models and the proficiency of the drawing artists. The findings from these studies led us to identify the current limitations of the proposed approach and suggest potential avenues for future development, including the utilization of more advanced 3D models as input and the incorporation of additional drawing representations. Additionally, we released the source code of the developed methods to facilitate future research in this area. To support further inquiry, we also provided access to the dataset utilized in the studies and the captured VR drawings. Observations using the James Webb Space Telescope will soon take advantage of this planet's extraordinary environment to study various aspects of its atmosphere. Additionally, they obtained new velocity measurements which were combined with the transit data, ultimately leading to a more precise estimate of the planet's orbital path. As a result, the margin of error for predicting transit and eclipse times has been reduced to 1-3 minutes. This new ephemeris will enable scientists to schedule JWST observations with a high level of accuracy, ensuring that they capture the planet's atmosphere during the exact moments of its scorching temperatures. Using the Iyer-Wald formalism, we have developed a comprehensive method for determining corrections to the mass and angular momentum of extreme black holes following various matter perturbations. This method explicitly calculates the minimal corrections in terms of horizon area and spin. Specifically, we have found that in the case of an initial state consisting of an extremal black hole with no charge, the leading correction to the mass is inversely proportional to the distance from the horizon, while the leading correction to the spin is dominated by the contribution of the electric potential. Additionally, we have derived a condition under which these corrections become negligible, finding that this outcome is consistent with the findings of Brown et al. for extremal black holes and of Hammann for near-extremal black holes. This work has been specialized to the case of gravitational perturbations and the results have been found to be in complete agreement with the predictions of previous studies. Furthermore, we have extended the Iyer-Wald analysis to the study of near-extremal black holes with non-zero charge. In this context, we have derived a condition under which the corrections to the mass and angular momentum can be accurately approximated using the simplest form of the Iyer-Wald prescription, finding that this approximation holds when the charge of the black hole is significantly smaller than its mass. This approximation has been further validated in the case of gravitational perturbations, where the resulting corrections to the mass and angular momentum were found to be in complete agreement with the predictions of previous studies. This work has also been specialized to the study of near-extremal black holes with zero charge. In this context, we have found that the Iyer-Wald analysis yields corrections to the mass and angular momentum that are proportional to the distance from the horizon, with the specific proportionality constant depending on the details of the perturbation. These findings have been further validated in the case of gravitational perturbations, where the resulting corrections to the mass and angular momentum were found to be in complete agreement with the predictions of previous studies. This work presents the first comprehensive application of the Iyer-Wald formalism to the study of corrections to the mass and angular momentum of black holes. In particular, we have focused on the detailed analysis of all possible terms in the formalism that contribute to these corrections, finding that the results can be accurately understood within the context of a simple, intuitive framework. This work also addresses a common misconception regarding the scope of the Iyer-Wald formalism, finding that the method is actually more versatile than previously thought

A major issue in current robotics research is enabling robots to acquire new skills through practice, a process known as motor learning. In contrast to human motor learning, which is often facilitated by intrinsic motivations to achieve accomplishments, robotics researchers often rely on external rewards and guidance to achieve this goal. This study proposes a novel and self-motivated approach to robot skill acquisition by exploring the underlying question of what robot goals are beneficial for learning new skills. We investigated three complementary objectives, including an intrinsic drive to achieve new state combinations, a social drive to improve others' outcomes, and an extrinsic drive to complete tasks efficiently. The results of our experiments demonstrated that these robotic goals can be pursued using a straightforward controller based on policy optimization and amenable to linear programming, and that they facilitate diverse forms of skill learning, including the emergence of novel plan elements and dynamic propulsive motions. This study provides a significant contribution to robotics research by identifying viable and easily implementable motivations for robot skill acquisition. Moreover, our findings on the characteristics of robotic goals are general and can be applied to a broad range of domains in artificial intelligence, including multi-agent scenarios, where the distribution of tasks and resources becomes a vital area of research. With its self-motivated approach to robot skill acquisition, this study may also spark fresh perspectives on human motor learning and the underlying mechanisms of human behavior. The developed controllers are now available in an open-source repository, enabling readers to reproduce the results and explore the various combinations of robotic drives. Furthermore, our website features additional content, including videos, as well as simulation tools that enable researchers to design and evaluate robotic goals and motors learning strategies in advanced environments. These resources come with a built-in discount rate filter to facilitate the comparison of robotic motors on an equal basis. The underlying software of these tools is based on the popular Robot Operating System and can be easily adapted to develop new and innovative robotic motors. Lastly, we examined the extent to which our intrinsic and extrinsic drives can be estimated from task performance using models of state visitation and policy evaluation, which demonstrated that social motors can be accurately inferred but the other motors cannot. This study may also be of interest to researchers in affective computing who are seeking to model and simulate human motivations. Additionally, our work on emergent plan elements may be of particular interest to researchers in autonomous systems who are seeking to simulate and model robotic behaviors. In vision-based robotic navigation, the effectiveness of learning approaches largely depends on their ability to store and retrieve memorable experiences effectively. Despite existing methods that train a single model to both collect and utilize environmental observations, we uncover that experiences collected in such a manner are often insufficient for successfully navigating previously unexplored areas. In response, we propose a new method, referred to as MemoNav, which treats experience collection and navigation as distinct tasks. The latter involves utilizing pre-collected memories, stored in a memory bank, through a attention-based mechanism that selectively retrieves relevant experiences. In contrast to traditional methods that train a single model to collect and navigate, we demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method by successfully applying it to complex, real-world navigation tasks. Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art navigation methods by achieving an average increase of 10.3% in success rates in experiments conducted on RoboTurk platform. Additionally, we provide an analysis of the proposed method's performance using visual representation evaluation metrics. Our code is publicly available on GitHub repository. We examine whether there's a connection between the operator growth approach and the bath method in studying quantum dynamics within a driven and dissipative environment.  Our research reveals that, in certain situations, these two methods are interrelated.  Specifically, we find that the bath method can be seen as an application of the operator growth technique when the system is a qubit.  Additionally, we generalize the operator growth approach to include non-perturbative interactions between the system and environment, and find that the bath method still retains a connection with this generalized theory.  Our work also explores the distinction between the system and the bath in the context of non-perturbative interactions, and identifies key characteristics that distinguish them.  Furthermore, we derive a specific formula for the bath density operator in the context of non-perturbative interactions, and find that it aligns with existing research.  Our study does, however, leave room for further investigation regarding the full generalized theory.  We speculate that it may be possible to develop a consistent and predictive theory of quantum dynamics using the operator growth approach, and encourage others to join in this research endeavor.  We also note that, in certain situations, the operator growth approach enables us to study quantum dynamics using solely the properties of the system in question, entirely dispense with any knowledge of the bath, and conclude that the system evolves independently.  This finding has significant implications that warrant further exploration.  We suggest that the differences between various approaches to studying operator growth may hold the key to unlocking a deeper understanding, and encourage others to join in this research endeavor.  We propose that one potential area of focus for additional research is the relationship between the system and its surroundings, and how it affects the system's behavior, and encourage others to explore this question.  We also note that our study may have simplified the process of studying quantum dynamics in complex systems by identifying key characteristics that affect the system's behavior, and encourage others to join in this research endeavor.  We demonstrate how the operator growth approach can be applied to study a real-world example, a crystal lattice driven by laser light.  We find that the system exhibits transitions between different patterns of behavior, and are able to accurately predict the system's behavior with high precision.  We also note that our study may have revealed new insights into the system's underlying structure.  We observe that the system's behavior is comprised of interconnected pieces, and propose that these pieces may be related to distinct parts of the system's underlying structure. The atomic structure of the Hoyle state, a state consisting of highly clustered $\alpha$ particles at 7.65 MeV in $^{12}\mathrm{C}$, has been a topic of interest for a long time. The question of whether this system consists of three weakly interacting $\alpha$ particles in the 0s orbital is crucial and can be answered by measuring the momentum distribution of the decay particles from the Hoyle state through the use of a Time Projection Chamber. By simulating different angular distributions of the decay particles, the momentum distribution of the single $\alpha$ particle component of the Hoyle state has been determined. The experimental results are consistent with the theoretical angular distribution and the cross-section of the $\mathrm{^{12}C}$($^8$Be, $^8$Be)$^{12}\mathrm{C}$ reaction, and the obtained distribution is in agreement with the previously published data from the in-flight experiment. The fraction of the non-emitting component in the Hoyle state, 81.8(3.0)%, has been calculated by using the measured beam intensity, the detected counts, and the angular distributions. The obtained distribution is wider than the previously measured distribution by the in-flight experiment. The data are also consistent with the prediction that the non-emitting component decreases with increasing bombarding energy. The observed variation in the momentum distribution is likely the result of the changed angular distributions of the direct decay component and the non-emitting $^8$Be state, as the Hoyle state is produced through the $^8$Be($^4$He, $^4$He)$^{12}\mathrm{C}$ reaction. The kinetic energy of the emerging $\alpha$ particles would increase as the production angular distribution becomes wider. The present result is the first measurement of the direct decay component of the Hoyle state with the Time Projection Chamber, and the obtained distribution is in agreement with the previously published data from the in-flight experiment. The distinction between the single $\alpha$ particle decay and the cluster decay of the Hoyle state has been made successfully by using the TPB detector, which is capable of measuring the momentum distribution of the decay particles. The result has further evidence for the predominant decay of the Hoyle state via the single $\alpha$ particle component. A theoretical model has been developed to analyze the behavior of a 2D Bose system with attractive interactions and exposed to a spatially varying harmonic potential and a periodic potential. This model is based on the Rashba Hamiltonian and is an extension of the Baskaran-Chen theory for spin-orbit coupled systems. It is found that under specific conditions, a spin-orbit coupling value above a certain threshold leads to the formation of a topological superfluid with spin polarization, whereas a lower value of the spin-orbit coupling results in a spin-depolarized topological superfluid. In the regime where the system exhibits multiple harmonic potential levels, a weak periodic potential can induce a transition to a topological superfluid from a Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer superfluid state. This model's application to ultracold atom experiments is also explored. One potential experiment involves creating a spin-orbit coupled Bose-Einstein condensate and trapping it in an optical lattice, followed by the adjustment of the Rashba interaction to enter the topological superfluid regime. Another possible experiment could involve tuning the Rashba interaction to a point where the system undergoes a transition from a Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer superfluid to a topological superfluid through the injection of fermionic holes. Additionally, a spin polarized topological superfluid could be generated by exposing a Bose-Einstein condensate with intrinsic spin polarization to a Gaussian wave function and then shaping it into a ring using a laser beam, followed by the adjustment of the Rashba interaction to enter the topological superfluid regime. One key challenge for these proposed experiments is determining an accurate value for the required Rashba interaction strength. In the case of the fermonic Rashba system, a preferred value for the spin-orbit coupling constant based on experimental estimates for lithium gas is provided. However, the required value for the Bose system needs to be investigated further. One possible method to determine this value is by comparing it to the estimated value for a similar system based on the Baskaran-Chen theory and the estimated value for a system with pure Rashba interaction. Additionally, the effect of different spin-orbit coupling schemes on the system needs to be studied to determine the optimal experimental conditions. In the event that the required Rashba interaction strength exceeds the capacity for practical implementation, the possibility of reducing the system to a one-dimensional system could be explored. This study focuses on understanding and interpreting tables, enabling researchers to draw inferences about relationships among cells. We introduce a new set of challenges, SEM-TAB-Facts, consisting of three sub-tasks: fact identification, fact verification, and evidence location. For sub-task A, participants classified whether a fact was accurate; in sub-task B, they verified whether a specific cell contained accurate information; and in sub-task C, they located the table cell supporting a given premise. A total of 56 teams from 16 countries submitted 1,095 teams (including cross-sub-task and cross-language combinations) to the three sub-tasks, and the winning submissions were announced with top performers receiving awards. With data available for public access, the experiment data can be found at https://github.com/aungkyee/SEM-TAB-Facts/tree/master/SharedTask-Data. Additionally, the team leader information has been updated and is now displayed on the SEM-TAB-Facts website. With a new initiative to organize workshops focused on actionable research, the project has secured funding to host its first seminar in Austin, Texas, U.S.A next March. We will provide more details on the project progress at the seminar.

In quantum mechanics, the unique properties of complex numbers are often implicitly assumed in formulas and calculations, with little discussion of their underlying assumptions. This lack of exploration has led to confusion and competing interpretations of the theory. By scrutinizing the mathematical framework of quantum mechanics, we reveal that the use of complex numbers is indeed essential. However, our analysis also uncovers a critical limitation: certain measurement devices can only be represented as complex-valued functions. The nature of this representational requirement remains elusive and implies that quantum mechanics is inherently inductive. Following a detailed examination of the respective epistemological architectures of real and complex number systems, we conclude that the real number realm is indeed insufficient to model quantum behavior. Consequently, any attempt to reform quantum mechanics into a real number-based theory from the ground up is bound to fail. Nonetheless, there is hope for modifications that would allow a more intuitive understanding of quantum phenomena using existing number systems. One such possibility involves adopting a complex-valued measurement theory for classical systems, thereby providing a more comprehensive and inclusive epistemological structure for the real number realm. Another possibility is to incorporate a complex number-based metadata layer in quantum mechanics, effectively treating certain quantum properties as inherently complex-valued. Ultimately, our analysis suggests that any satisfactory interpretation of quantum mechanics must acknowledge and accommodate the inherent complexities of quantum measurements. In contrast, common interpretations that try to understand quantum mechanics within the real number realm, such as the many-worlds theory or ontological theories, are inherently flawed. Similarly, ontological theories that reduce quantum mechanics to a real number-based dynamics are doomed to fail. Furthermore, our analysis implies that deformed or noncommutative quantum mechanics will inevitably involve complex numbers. Lastly, our analysis suggests that any future quantum theories, including quantum gravity, will require a similar epistemological architecture. In contrast, alternative theories such as dynamical reduction theories and spontaneous collapse theories are inherently flawed. The metric dimension of a graph G = (V, E) is the minimum number of vertices that can locate every other vertex using their shortest path distances. A proposed metric, 'r', determines the topological distance between pairs of vertices in G. For a given graph, choosing 'r' smallest enough to distinguish between all pairs of vertices determines the graph's metric dimension. Let the smallest such 'r' be denoted as the metric dimension number, and assume a positive integer 't' is less than or equal to 'r'. Here, the 't'-trimmed metric dimension of G is the minimum number of vertices that can identify and determine the distance 'r' to at least t other vertices. A method has been developed to calculate the 1-trimmed metric dimension for all finite graphs, which represents a solution to a previously unstated problem in the field. The approach uses the concept of geodesic closed paths in a graph to establish a relationship between the 1-trimmed and traditional metric dimension. In particular, it is claimed that the 1-trimmed dimension of a graph G is equal to its usual metric dimension, provided that the graph contains no vertices with a distance of 2 from the shortest path to another vertex. A related property has also been proposed, where a graph's '2-convexity' represents the topological structure in which every pair of vertices is within twice the shortest path distance apart. It has been shown that the 1-trimmed dimension of a 2-convex graph represents half the graph's usual metric dimension dimension. Additionally, specific methods have been developed to calculate the 1-trimmed dimension for certain types of planar graphs. In particular, it has been shown that the 1-trimmed dimension of a tree graph is equal to its usual metric dimension, unless the tree contains a specific topological structure with three vertices connected to a common vertex. A proposed approach has been developed to calculate the 1-trimmed dimension for all trees with this specific structure, which may be extended to a more general method in the future. Furthermore, distinct algorithms have been devised to determine the 1-trimmed dimension for certain types of bipartite graphs. The removal of sulfur dioxide from flue gas using an ozone/UV light system has been evaluated under various conditions in a laboratory study. Ozone injection quantities, UV lamp intensity, temperature, and recirculation rates were investigated in a well-mixed reactor to determine their impact on SOx removal. Ozone consumption was also examined using a photochemical model, OZON/CHEM, which was developed to analyze the dependences of these factors. Research demonstrated that SOx removal efficiency increases with rising ozone doses and UV light intensity, but is highly dependent on temperature, declining with increased recirculation rates. A temperature change of 10 Celsius affects UV sensitivity, but a comprehensive assessment reveals the best economic results are achieved at temperatures between 30 and 40 degrees Celsius. A comprehensive evaluation of various scenarios identifies the optimal conditions as a 40 mg/Nm3 ozone dose, 4 watts/cm2 UV light intensity, and a recirculation rate of 3, which yields a 98% SOx removal efficiency, accompanied by a 88% ozone consumption efficiency. Moreover, this study confirms the practical applicability of the developed model, OZON/CHEM, in predicting ozone consumption and system performance. A comparative financial analysis shows the most economical approach to S02 removal is a combination of the ozone/UV light system and a scrubber, outperforming other technologies like the catalytic converter and ClO2 method. Valuable insights from this study can guide the design and optimization of a novel sulfur dioxide removal plant using an ozone/UV light system. It also provides important information for evaluating the performance of existing systems using ozone/UV light technology for SOx removal. Furthermore, this research confirms the importance of recirculating gas in reducing ozone consumption and system costs, as well as lengthening the system's maintenance cycle. Recirculation rates are suggested to be set at 3-4 for the best economic results. A comparison of different control strategies reveals the best performance is achieved by adjusting ozone doses based on the system's current condition, leading to reduced consumption and emissions. This study also confirms UV light integrity and long life with proper protection, making ozone/UV light low-cost and efficient method for sulfur dioxide removal in practice. It's also a reliable and emissions-free technology for the future. This research provides critical information for designing and optimizing a low-temperature flue gas treatment system using an ozone/UV light system. It also compares the performance of different treatment systems, including oxygen-containing systems, and provides crucial guidelines

As interest in neuromorphic computing grows, engineers face a key challenge in simulating the technology to evaluate and refine their designs. Traditional simulation tools have limitations, such as inaccurate physical modeling and system-level simulation capabilities. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes a concurrent simulation framework that enables efficient modeling of complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor circuits and novel neuromorphic computing architectures at the system-level. The framework is based on the SystemC standard and is demonstrated through the simulation of a specific neurocore architecture. The results show that the proposed framework significantly reduces simulation time by leveraging hardware concurrency, outperforming conventional full-system simulation methods. The performance of the simulated microelectronic circuit was also accurately predicted using the proposed framework. The study highlights the feasibility of the proposed framework in modeling various neural network architectures and identifies potential areas for improvement. The developed framework has been made available on the GitHub platform for public access. The corresponding user manual is available under the name SCNC-UOS and can be accessed via the link https://github.com/hci-uos/SCNC-UOS/tree/master/docs. Moreover, the developed framework is integrated into the open-source emulator emuNC for neuromorphic computing platforms, which can also be found on the link https://github.com/hci-uos/emun c. emuNC/tree/master/docs. The proposed framework paves the way for the use of traditional hardware description languages in developing emulators for next-generation neuromorphic computing platforms. The integration of the proposed framework into the emuNC emulator enables the efficient simulation of various architectures, such as spiking-invariant neural network, crossbar, neurogrid, and truenorth. Furthermore, the study explores two key areas for improving the proposed framework: the concurrent execution of SystemC processes and the efficient modeling of memory components within the emuNC emulator. The results show that the proposed framework significantly enhances the simulation capacity by hardware concurrency, while also improving the efficiency of the emuNC emulator by hardware concurrency and optimal memory modeling. Machine learning models are typically employed to make a single prediction, yet often produce multi-valued outcomes and can be viewed as generating arguments to support predicted results. Decision forests, a widely used model, are particularly suitable for this perspective due to their interpretability and decision-making structure. Focusing on classification tasks, we introduce the concept of Indecision Forests by encapsulating classification models within a probabilistic argumentation framework called Indecision Theory. This framework assigns confidence levels to arguments and their combinations, defining the plausibility of arguments to be weaker than their components. We show that Decision Forests can be viewed as InDecision Forests and that learning under quantified uncertainty leads to improved performance in tasks such as distributional shift, adversarial attacks, and adversarial teaching, outperforming conventional Decision Forests and other top-notch machine learning models. Additionally, we propose a novel metric for evaluating the consistency of machine learning arguments and provide an in-depth analysis of its behavior. Importantly, our work highlights that augmenting Decision Forests with uncertainty quantification does not impair but rather enhances their effectiveness. Therefore, we advocate for incorporating quantified uncertainty into the Indecision Forests framework to foster innovative research in this area. The proposed approach offers a ground-breaking understanding of how arguments within Decision Forests function and could have significant implications in data-driven argumentation techniques. A public demonstration of the model's capabilities is available at https://public.iaicommunity.org/project/indecision-forests-u4lm/overview. This includes the code for the Indecision Forests library, which is compatible with scikit-learn, and a range of predefined models. Furthermore, we have made available the code for the experiments described in the paper, which can be accessed via https://github.com/iai-aii/indecision-forests/tree/main/evaluation. Nevertheless, DTW's high computational cost hindering its practical use in several scenarios. PrunedDTW and its improved variants were developed to optimize DTW's efficiency, yet they still fall short in handling large datasets within main memory constraints, especially when queries exceed samples. To address this, we introduce an approach enhancing PrunedDTW-based methods, allowing for early discarding of unfeasible alignments during the DTW computation. Current testing methods prioritize thoroughness over efficiency, leading to expanded test suites and increased testing time. In contrast, research on educational testing has shown limited success. To address this, we introduce inquiry-based testing, a more conceptual approach that encourages flexible testing methods and efficient resource usage. This study compares traditional and conceptual teaching methods within a testing course, examining the impact on student learning, testing habits, and professional practices. An online survey of 29 students in a testing course found that conceptual teaching resulted in higher test coverage and fewer used testing tools compared to traditional methods. Additionally, students in the conceptual group demonstrated improved performance in a practical exercise and a professional certification exam. Further analysis revealed that conceptual teaching led to increased adoption of modern testing techniques, including theory-guided testing methods, and improved understanding of testing artifacts, ultimately resulting in higher overall test quality. Overall, this study indicates that conceptual teaching is an effective approach for teaching testing, particularly when working with real-world projects and testing tools. Based on the findings, we present a theoretical model illustrating the key factors contributing to the success of conceptual teaching in testing education. Furthermore, this study highlights the practical advantages of conceptual teaching, including reduced testing-related time and increased efficiency in educational settings. To further investigate the effectiveness of this approach, we propose a set of recommendations for evaluating the conceptual teaching model through repeatable and controllable empirical research. By doing so, we aim to contribute to the development of evidence-based learning methods in software testing education. Keywords: Software Testing, Educational Testing, Inquiry-Based Testing, Thorough Testing, Testing Education, Empirical Investigation.

In domains requiring reliability or transparency, explainable AI is increasingly becoming essential for handling the unpredictability of black-box machine learning methods, particularly in healthcare and data protection regulations. However, standard visualizations often fall short due to their inability to differentiate between subtle feature variations or accurately represent the interplay between absent and present features. This issue could be addressed by using more sophisticated symbolic surrogate models but, since these typically demand symbolic inputs not commonly available in computer vision, we instead explore a new method: utilizing intrinsic network features to explain outgoing network data through symbolic regression. This approach, although straightforward, poses significant challenges: (1) how to effectively represent intricate network properties and (2) how to merge these representations with the inherent complexities of the learning problem via induction. This study addresses these challenges by employing an innovative two-step process that first employs a deep generative network to generate distinctive feature sets, then uses these derived features, along with the explanations generated by the network, and perturbation analysis, in a symbolic regression system via Inductive Logic Programming to establish a complete explanation. This method was successfully tested on the Tabular Q-learning problem and two computer vision problems: explaining image classification and object detection. The results show that our approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods, with human and automated evaluation indicating its symbolic nature and use of intrinsic features to generate precise and generalizable explanations. The implementation of this method, along with the symbolic surrogate models, is available on GitHub at https://github.com/SebastianMontalban/ExSy. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods by up to 11\%, with an average improvement of 3\%, in various computer vision and healthcare applications. The symbolic nature of our method also leads to more accurate and generalizable outcomes, along with increased human understanding. The use of intrinsic features and ILP enables our approach to surpass current methods by providing more comprehensive and generalizable explanations for DNNs. The graph convolutional neural network has emerged as a pivotal component in machine learning for graph data, playing a critical role in graph node classification. Despite its success, the Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) has a fundamental limitation that hampers its further development. The existing methods to improve GCN performance, such as stacking multiple GCN layers, often lead to the over-blurring issue, where the performance deteriorates significantly. The root cause of this problem is the repeated amplification of errors in subsequent GCN layers. In this context, we address the over-blurring issue of GCN by introducing a novel approach called Error Enhancement Network (EEN), which enables the error propagation of each GCN layer to supplement the information of adjacent layers. The EEN enables effective information distillation, where the error propagation from a lower layer is magnified to enhance the representation of adjacent layers. The proposed EEN has a key advantage of enriching the representation without requiring the accumulation of errors, thus disabling the over-blurring issue. Theoretical analysis and experiments demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, which outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in node classification for citation networks and PPI networks. Data was collected between 2016 and 2018 at a center of mass energy of 13 TeV using the CMS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider, equating to 137 fb^-1 of integrated luminosity. By examining two distinct particle decays – one involving electron pairs and the other muon pairs – researchers find that their observations match expected standard model behavior. Specifically, they set new limits on the interaction strength of dark matter particles with other particles, as well as their involvement in Z boson generation, with certain scenarios seeing increased constraints of up to 30% and new areas of constraint being established. Furthermore, these researchers set limits on theoretical models that involve dark matter interacting with Higgs bosons, extra dimensions, and mediating particles, among others, often seeing their original predictions surpassed by the CMS data. Lastly, while this study does not yield direct evidence of dark matter, it establishes competitive new constraints on dark matter-related phenomena and expands upon existing knowledge of the underlying physics. The research also provides groundwork for future dark matter explorations, potentially including new areas such as monophoton and inverted mass scenarios. The data is made accessible in the CMS publication database and is also reflected in the Review of Particle Physics.
