We investigate how the parity-time symmetry in a finite lattice affects the light-matter interaction model based on the Purcell effect, using a rigorous mathematical approach. By employing the measure-theoretic paradigm, we define and differentiate between open and closed systems, and identify the essential conditions for parity-time symmetry in a finite lattice to be realized. Furthermore, we develop a strict mathematical representation of the radiation rate and prove its measure-invariant property with respect to any unitary transformation preserving the parity-time symmetry. This generalizes and reinforces the invariance of the radiation rate under spatial reflections and complex conjugation, as previously established findings. We further demonstrate that this invariance holds not only for the tight-binding model but also for any model based on a first-principle tight-binding framework. We illustrate the validity of our approach through a numerical example, where we calculate the radiation rate for a dimer model positioned within an infinite and a finite waveguide, and show that despite a visible difference in the system's wave function, the measure-invariant theory predicts a comparable radiation rate in both scenarios. This theoretical framework provides a precise and generalized interpretation of the parity-time symmetry in the context of light-matter interactions, and we anticipate that it will significantly contribute to the development of innovative optical devices. We also envision that this theoretical framework will enable the exploration of new ideas in optical engineering, where the concept of a 'effective Hamiltonian' may no longer be applicable, as traditionally assumed based on a first-principle tight-binding model. Ultimately, we anticipate that this theoretical framework will enable us to devise new strategies for controlling and engineering the light-matter interaction, perhaps by deliberately introducing a finite waveguide and selecting its dimensions in a way that maximizes the radiation rate and achieves a specified order of magnitude. Such a design approach could potentially lead to the creation of innovative devices, such as those for nanoscale laser development, that would be impossible to achieve based on the existing understanding of parity-time symmetry. In summary, we believe that the measure-invariant theory of light-matter interactions presents a novel and interesting perspective on this topic, and that it presents numerous opportunities for the development of innovative optical devices. We anticipate that this measure-invariant perspective will be particularly useful in exploring new orders of magnitude in optical interactions, and that it may no longer be applicable to our current understanding of devices, such as antennas and photonic waveguides. In that regard, we believe that the measure-invariant theory of light-matter interactions presents a new and interesting paradigm for optical research and development

A new clinical trial design known as the basket trial has emerged as a viable option for assessing the effectiveness of targeted therapies in genetically identified patient subgroups. This design involves running a single trial protocol that involves multiple subgroups or "baskets", which allow researchers to gather data more efficiently than traditional hierarchical phase II-III trials. In order to optimize the statistical power of these trials, researchers have developed methods for assessing the required sample size needed to achieve a certain confidence level for a treatment effect. However, these methods typically assume that data from all baskets are equally relevant and that observations within each basket are independent and normally distributed. This paper explores alternative methods for assessing the required sample size that take into account observations within each basket as being mutually dependent and rank-based observations. Two case studies are also presented to demonstrate how these methods can be applied in real-world scenarios. The case studies involve simulations of two basket trials designed for assessing the effectiveness of targeted therapies in specific genetic conditions. The results show that the proposed methods perform better than existing methods when data from multiple baskets are combined. To meet the demands of cutting-edge technology, motion control systems require considerable enhancements in accuracy, speed, and robustness. This has driven the development of linear parameter-varying (LPV) feedback controllers, which offer a solution to improving performance in these systems. However, the complexity of LPV design poses a significant challenge, primarily due to the need for precise and frequently changing system state information. To address these concerns in this study, the authors propose a innovative sequential loop tightening (SLT) approach for LPV feedback controller design. The proposed method partitions the controller design into simpler sub-systems and applies LPV techniques to each component, which significantly reduces the requirement for precise system state information. Furthermore, the authors implement a robust control strategy to ensure stability and performance across a range of conditions. To minimize processing demands, the authors also explore and implement fixed-point versions of the controller. To verify the efficacy of this method, the proposed controller design is evaluated on a high-precision motion system, specifically a Theta motion table, which is then put to the test in practical experiments. The results show that the proposed controller design successfully achieves high-precision and robust motion, which is also reflected in the experimental findings. Additionally, the fixed-point implementation of the controller demonstrates satisfactory performance, which is an essential consideration for real-world applications. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this study presents the first-ever LPV feedback controller design for the Theta motion system, which is also believed to be the first LPV controller to be evaluated on this specific system. The proposed controller design is anticipated to contribute significantly to the advancement of motion control systems in industry and academic settings. Leveraging deep learning's ability to handle complex relationships, PRNet focuses on predicting a complete 3D model from input partial clouds. To ensure precise alignment, PRNet learns to ignore irrelevant geometric features and concentrate on both duplicate and same-object partial clouds. The primary sound source in audio recording is generally considered to be emissions from the recorder itself, excluding external acoustic pickups. However, in practical recording scenarios, another significant sound source exists - the ground sound - which is often disregarded despite causing distortion and signal contamination. This paper aims to address the significance of ground sound, particularly in GPR technology, by which its impact can be minimized through optimal antenna placement, thereby creating a usable signal reference point. The approach involves using ground sound as a reliable sound source anchor, enabling the separation of sound signals from their unwanted attachments. This strategy has been successfully implemented in various recording situations, exemplified by its effectiveness in monitoring Harriet Mwadime's expedition sounds in Kenya. mwadime_experiments

The effect of ground sound was discovered during experiments in Kenya, where a rich response was obtained despite the expedition's vehicle being at least 15 meters away from the recorder. Upon examination, it became apparent that the recorder was picking up sounds from the engine and its surroundings through its external acoustic pickup, which was then mixed with the ground sound. Interestingly, a comparable response was achieved by placing the external pickup onto the ground, effectively utilizing the ground sound as the primary sound source. This surprising finding was further verified using a controlled setup in a local park, where the recorder was placed over a resonating leaf-covered ground surface, producing a detailed representation of the leaves' pattern in audio waveform. Consequently, the ground sound has been recognized as a highly responsive and adaptive sound source anchor, offering numerous theoretical and practical research opportunities. The incorporation of ground sound recording could significantly contribute to research in signal processing, acoustic imaging, and biophony. In particular, it may enable the creation of highly detailed environmental sound maps using the ground sound as a signal reference point. Furthermore, the ground sound recording approach could be adapted for use in GPR technology, enhancing its spatial resolution by effectively utilizing the ground's responsive properties. Lastly, the ground sound approach may also hold potential for applications in audio technology and music production, including the generation of novel, environmentally-synchronized sounds and the development of more accurate algorithmic music systems. Ultimately, the ground sound, when harnessed, offers a wealth of previously unrecognized possibilities for sound signal processing and environmental understanding.

One key limitation of recommender systems is data scarcity resulting in considerable variability. Multiple approaches have been implemented to address this issue including the integration of human-generated content, content-based methods, and fusion of disparate recommendation techniques. Within the context of research focused on addressing variability, this paper introduces a novel hybrid recommender system that integrates elements of document context-based and behavior-based methods. By incorporating rich user-generated content and combining it with collaborative filtering, this hybrid model offers a more comprehensive learning environment. Furthermore, this paper undertakes an in-depth examination of various deep learning architectures to support the training of this hybrid system within a single unified framework. The integrated method is rigorously evaluated on two real-world datasets, demonstrating superior effectiveness and state-of-the-art performance in terms of stability. Meanwhile, an open-source implementation of this model is accessible via GitHub at the specified link. Ultimately, this hybrid approach is presented as an enhanced method to address the issue of variability in recommender systems and can be adapted in various other domains. Experimental results show that it surpasses existing hybrid systems and achieves the best results to date. Key findings include a substantial enhancement of 6.58% and 16.33% in terms of effectiveness, as well as a significant reduction of 14.53% and 30.42% in terms of variability, relative to the best existing hybrid systems in the domains of movies and books. In terms of explanation, the integrated model was found to significantly reduce the reliance on human-generated content by 121.14%, while also decreasing its reliance on user-item interaction by 55.31%. These compelling results highlight the ability of this hybrid model to effectively address the issue of variability through a combination of human-generated content and collaborative filtering. Consequently, this hybrid model offers a more stable, effective, and diverse solution for recommender systems seeking to address variability. We present here the characterization results of the chosen GRAVITY assembly, focusing on the performance of its camera assembly, and detailing the intrinsic resolution, image stabilization, and phasing accuracy capabilities. Additionally, we address the implications of these results on the overall instrument performance during early science operations.

Based on a point-charged model, the proposed expression accurately accounts for the electrostatic interactions among both identical and dissimilar atoms, across all relevant distances. In contrast to existing theories, this framework considers a comprehensive set of quantum states without resorting to approximations such as linearization or expansion. By incorporating a mathematical function representing the overall charge density of the alkali metal vapor, the proposed model derives analytical expressions for key thermodynamic parameters, including the free energy, entropy, and heat capacity. Furthermore, this framework is used to analyze and calculate key physical characteristics, including the effective number of particles, radial distribution function, and energy partitioning among particles at varying temperatures. Moreover, this model's predictions show excellent agreement with existing empirical data and simulations. In particular, the predicted temperature dependence of the partitioning coefficient matches the experimental results with an error margin of less than 5%. Additionally, the predicted radial distribution functions and entropy values align closely with the results of molecular dynamics simulations. Finally, this analysis demonstrates that the phase transition characteristics of the proposed model can be accurately described using a simplified version of the Gibbs free energy change, thereby elucidating the underlying physics of the phase transition and confirming that the resulting pressure profile exhibits a saddle-point structure, consistent with experimental observations. Overall, this analytical framework is the first to successfully model the equilibrium behavior of alkali metals without relying on approximations and demonstrates the importance of considering electrostatic interactions among identical and dissimilar atoms. Furthermore, this framework's simplicity makes it highly suitable for computational purposes, as evidenced by the excellent agreement between its predictions and the results of other methods. Additionally, this study verifies that the principles of quantum statistics, encompassing both the Bose-Einstein and Fermi-Dirac distributions, contribute to a deep understanding of the alkali metal's behavior. Finally, the proposed model's expressions for entropy and the partitioning coefficient highlight the inherent inaccuracies of classical statistical theories, as these predictions are superior to those obtained using these simpler statistical models. On the other hand, the proposed model's predictions for the free energy and heat capacity are not significantly improved over the predictions of simpler models. Nonetheless, this study showcases the capabilities of the proposed analytical framework in modeling the equilibrium behavior of alkali metals. Potential future developments of this model may involve extending its applications to model the behavior of other elements. Additionally, the proposed model could be used to simulate the behavior of alkali earth and group 16 elements

Predicting time series in multiple dimensions is a common challenge in systems and design, yet there's a lack of research on adapting complex models to fit complex systems. This paper introduces a pioneering Neural Network model, Adaptive GCN, specifically designed for multidimensional time series forecasting by incorporating the principles of graph theory. By dynamically creating connections between dimensions based on historical dependencies, the Adaptive GCN model is able to learn various patterns, including shifting, oscillating, and other common signal types. This framework is versatile and can be applied to a range of systems, such as modeling energy consumption in high-dimensional space. Experimental results show that the Adaptive GCN model outperforms existing methods by significantly reducing mean absolute prediction error (MAPe) for systems with up to five dimensions. Notably, the Adaptive GCN model achieved a 20% improvement in MAPe compared to a basic multivariate AR model for a real-world energy consumption dataset. Additionally, the Adaptive GCN model performed well in comparison to state-of-the-art deep learning models, indicating its effectiveness in adapting complex systems through innovative graph structure configurations. A public code repository for the Adaptive GCN model has been set up at https://github.com/Ashtiyani/Adaptive-GCN. In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocity or momentum. Nevertheless, the standard lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements tend to suffer from numerical errors in reconstructing the vector transport equation. This drawback is particularly noticeable when simulating regions with complex geometries or multiple dimensions. Fortunately, recent advancements have proposed various strategies to improve the accuracy of the transported quantity on any given mesh. This work aims to introduce and evaluate the performance of four distinct correction methods, applying them to both linear and nonlinear transport equations in multiple dimensions. Furthermore, we compute the optimal discrete tensor for transporting vector-valued fields on quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements, both in two and three dimensions. Our studies validate the effectiveness of the proposed corrections, revealing significant post-processing improvements in scenarios of varied complexity. Additionally, we confirm that the reconstructed tensor's performance approaches the optimal discrete tensor as the discrete tensor tends towards its perfect counterpart. This work is expected to contribute to efforts to perfect transport schemes for simulating fluid dynamics, especially in complex multi-dimensional settings. The development of decentralized machine learning techniques such as federated learning is crucial for maintaining confidentiality of sensitive data. In this study, we bridge a gap in current research by investigating whether federated learning can be effectively combined with fairness metrics and differential privacy constraints. To achieve this, we draw upon the connection between expected gradient estimates and the Poisson distribution, establishing a framework for modeling stochastic gradient approximations. This framework enables us to devise novel approaches for designing fairness-constrained minimization problems and differential privacy-encouraged regularization techniques under various FL settings. Experimental results, performed using synthetic data in scalar and matrix format, demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed methods. Furthermore, we examine the interplay between fairness and differential privacy, discovering that their interaction has unexpected outcomes. This research presents the first investigation into combining fairness and differential privacy within FL, along with the lowest known privacy cost for achieving certain performance levels in fairness-based FL, measured by the Earth Mover's Distance. Our code is publicly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/jbodnar1/Federated-learning-adversarial-privacy-fairness. In model-parallel training of deep neural networks, distributing neural network layers across multiple GPUs can significantly reduce computational expenses. However, the limitations of communication bandwidth in distributed learning often lead to a bottleneck in achieving full computational parallelization. To overcome this challenge, we propose a novel approach called regional critic training, which involves locally normalizing the gradients collected from each GPU node with a layer-specific normalization factor. By doing so, we reduce the size of communication data while concurrently addressing vanishing gradient issues through gradient normalization. Experimental results on a range of state-of-the-art network architectures demonstrate that regional critic training effectively alleviates communication parallelism bottlenecks and enables full computational parallelization without additional costs. The proposed method is versatile, supporting different hardware configurations, and can be applied to various deep learning applications with model-parallel learning. The code is openly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/hliang2019/RCT. The benchmark is openly available on the NetGPU repository https://netgpu.github.io.

Three-dimensional chaotic scattering has garnered interest due to its impacts on real-world phenomena, which are often influenced by dissipation. Interestingly, our findings reveal that weak dissipation enhances the Wada basins in the interior, while simultaneously creating an additional Wada basin on the boundary. Moreover, the number of escape routes through the boundary's surface in each Wada basin is increased by dissipation. Additionally, our calculations indicate that nearly all escape paths adopt a snaking route across three dimensional topological invariants known as the three-dimensional cable structure. A measure of escape rate is used to quantify the behaviors of Wada basins in systems with various dissipation values. It has been established that certain three-dimensional chaotic trajectories exhibit a form of topological memory, where the topological structure of the escape channel remains unchanged as dissipation varies. This concept is relevant to understanding the real-world implications of three dimensional chaotic scattering phenomena. Lastly, it is suggested that the occurrence of Wada basins in three dimensional systems may be prevalent due to the generation of secondary Wada basins via a 'glassy' mechanism. This could offer new insights into the generalized Wada phenomenon in any arbitrary dimension. Ultimately, this research contributes to existing knowledge on three dimensional Wada basins by revealing how weak dissipation affects the basins' topological structures and escapes through the boundary. Furthermore, it is found that the escapes are largely unified by their routes across three dimensional cables. Lastly, it is hypothesized that the generalized Wada basin in any arbitrary dimension may be constituted by the accumulation of infinitesimal Wada basins. With the development of more efficient computational tools, it may become possible to model this feedback in greater detail and gain a deeper understanding of its effects on future star creation. Ultimately, further research into the birth and death of stars is necessary to gain a more comprehensive understanding of the intricate processes that govern the life cycles of these celestial bodies. With the emergence of new capabilities and resource allocations, it may become possible to model the complex dynamics of star formation in greater detail and gain a more nuanced understanding of the processes that give rise to the vast arrays of stars that exist in our universe.

The central issue of glass dynamics, the boson peak, remains poorly understood despite extensive research. Recent studies using advanced neutron spectroscopy have made significant contributions to investigating the boson peak in various glasses. This work summarizes key findings from such studies, highlighting how they have shed light on the underlying dynamics of glassy materials. In particular, the application of spin-polarized inelastic neutron scattering has facilitated the differentiation of acoustic and optical phonons in measurements. Additionally, the use of transversely polarized exitation has enabled the determination of phonon polarization. A particular representation of preferences, known as additively separable, expresses an agent's preference as a sum of individual components rather than a comprehensive hierarchical list. In Section 2, guided by the guidance of Greenland and Benzi (2018), we engage in a detailed examination of the designated control approach proposed by Dukes and Vansteelandt (2020), and demonstrate that under specific assumptions, our target policy learning approach yields superior performance compared to their designated control approach. Additionally, we address raised concerns and questions in Section 3, and make relevant supplementary observations. In Section 4, guided by the style of Kallus (2020) and Dukes and Vansteelandt (2020), we conclude our rejoinder by reiterating the distinct research contributions, variations in assumptions, and approaches compared to prior works, and highlight the common research objectives, variations in assumptions, and approaches that lead to similar policy learning results between our target approach and the alternative control approach proposed by Dukes and Vansteelandt (2020). Furthermore, we conclude by identifying essential areas that require future research to investigate in a deeper manner. Our supplementary materials include a copy of our original article, proof of theoretical results, and a detailed simulation study examining the performance of both target and alternative control approaches. This supplementary materials can be accessed via the link provided at the end of this rejoinder. We express our gratitude to the discussants, editors, and reviewers for their valuable comments, and greatly appreciated the support from our colleagues and friends. We also extend our gratitude to the funders for funding our research, as listed at the end of this rejoinder. Finally, we express our heartfelt appreciation to my family for their unwavering support and selfless devotion.

Meta-analyses that incorporate study-specific covariate data to control classification bias when pooling effect sizes must address both bias and variance in the resulting estimates.  Consider a set of $m$ studies, with each study influenced by a unique set of covariates denoted as $\mathbf{W}_j$, and a given effect size $\tilde{Y}_{j\theta}$, where $\theta$ represents the vector of covariates relevant to each study $j$.  Under the assumption that studies can be grouped into $Q$ clusters based on shared covariates, a mixed-effects model that incorporates both within-study bias and between-study variance becomes applicable.  We refer to this type of model as the "mixed model with a random effect for meta-analytical units."  Estimating the parameters in this model is often referred to as a "mixed meta-analysis" approach and involves the use of Likelihood Ratio Tests and related measures for hypothesis testing and model evaluation.  Two primary variants of this estimator exist: the derivative-based "REML" approach and an "ML-RE" approach.  Both estimators have been widely utilized but have been shown to have both desirable and undesirable properties, including biases under certain data configurations.  A new family of cluster-robust estimators has been developed to address these biases and provide consistent results even in the presence of certain types of model misspecification.  The estimators in question achieve this by employing an $M$-estimation technique that utilizes a weighted influence function to eliminate bias while controlling variance.  A key characteristic of these estimators is the use of an asymptotic variance-covariance matrix, thereby accounting for both within-study residual variance and between-study variance.  A method for estimating this variance-covariance matrix is also discussed.  The proposed estimators have been shown to have several desirable properties, including being unbiased, consistent, and asymptotically normal under specific data configurations.  A method for assessing the significance of results has been developed, along with associated software implementations using both R and Python programming languages.  The proposed approach has been demonstrated to be a reliable alternative to existing estimators through simulations involving diverse data configurations, including scenarios involving small sample sizes and skewed distributions.  The efficiency of the proposed estimators has been compared to those of alternative estimators under various data configurations. To this end, we partition the black hole's mass into three components: the stationary, the accretion, and the hole itself. To resolve the unanswered questions from our previous work, we demonstrate that the accretion process must be accompanied by mass loss occurring at or near the event horizon. Consequently, the source of emitted quanta is not the stationary or hole components, but rather those created as incoming accretion matter dissipates. To substantiate our theory, we show that the Unruh/Hawking process can be mathematically represented as a change in the accretion process's energy, which is caused by the black hole's gravitational potential. Moreover, our analysis reveals the typical emission energy to be higher than the corresponding accretion energy, mainly due to the black hole's gravitational potential. The effect of nuclear parton distribution functions on the transverse momentum of hadrons produced in relativistic heavy-ion collisions is investigated using a Monte Carlo simulation based on the color dipole model. By comparing the resulting $p_T$ spectra obtained with different nuclear PDFs to data from the LHC, we observe that some nuclear PDFs significantly diverge from the corresponding proton distribution while others agree. Furthermore, we find that the outcome is sensitive to the model parameters used to generate the nuclear PDFs, and also to the process by which the partons acquire a transverse momentum in the final hadronization stage. Notably, our analysis indicates that some nuclear PDFs can even yield a higher $p_T$ spectrum than from proton PDFs, which could have implications for understanding the nature of parton interactions in the QCD plasma at high energy. Our work also highlights the necessity for more accurate constraints on nuclear PDFs that take into account, beyond mere PDF calculations, different physical mechanisms by which partons' properties in the QCD plasma are influenced. Such a understanding could be derived from the study of both PDFs themselves and the collective, anisotropic $p_T$ characteristics observed in ultrarelativistic heavy-ion collisions. In the context of the present investigation, we discovered that some nuclear PDFs are able to capture the observed, high $p_T$-induced anisotropy observed in the collisions, which is commonly attributed to the phenomena of collective flow and parton interactions within the QCD plasma. To further explore the relationship between nuclear PDFs and the $p_T$ spectrum, we propose an alternative approach, in which the relative contributions of partons from the nuclear and proton targets are weighed according to their respective probabilities, effectively averaging over the parton properties in the two nuclei. This approach leads to a significant reduction in the observed $p_T$ differences between nuclear and proton-induced spectra, which suggests that any remaining discrepancies are likely the result of parton interactions within the QCD plasma. In light of our findings, we suggest that future investigations into the $p_T$ spectrum in the regime of high energy and dense nuclei should prioritize distinguishing between various possible nuclear PDFs at low $p_T$, as well as clarifying the processes by which partons acquire a transverse momentum in the final hadronization stage. This article presents the complete set of integer solutions for the equation $a^2 + ab + b^2 = 7^n$, and confirms that the non-trivial solutions can be expressed as $(a, b) = (1, 3), (3, 1), (317, 199), (199, 317)$. It has been proven that no other non-trivial solutions exist. As an interesting observation, the solutions are limited to $a, b < 7^{n-1}$. The research was initially sparked by a mathematical competition question. The proof of non-rationality of $\sqrt[3]{7}$ led us to realize the potential of exploring similar equations based on the sum of three squares, and we were able to derive an explicit expression for such solutions. Although our investigation was focused on the specific equation $a^2 + ab + b^2 = 7^n$, the methods we developed are highly versatile and are likely to be adapted for generalising to other similar equations based on distinct prime numbers. The article also includes an appendix that presents an alternative proof of the non-rationality of $\sqrt[3]{7}$. This work presents an innovative application of their formula in the context of the three-body problem, using it to make accurate predictions about orbital periods and other characteristics, such as the final outcomes of encounters involving binary systems colliding with passing objects. By analyzing a large set of simulated encounters, our research shows that these predictions are largely accurate and identifies areas where the model needs to be refined. Notably, our analysis confirms that most encounters end in collisions, which aligns with previous studies. The next stage of our research will involve testing these predictions using real astronomical data to see how well the model fits observations from the field. This work has potential broader applications in other areas of physics, such as the dynamics of atoms and molecules. We propose a category $\mathcal{C}$ to capture the essence of continuous logic developed by Richard Dale, enabling the formation of a symmetric monoidal closed category. Our construction details a way to embed continuous logic spaces within $\mathcal{C}$ and demonstrate that the category adheres to established logic principles. In addition, we define a functor $\mathcal{C} \rightarrow \mathcal{P}$ that maps $\mathcal{C}$ onto the category $\mathcal{P}$ of proximity spaces, showing that the category is equivalent to $\mathcal{P}$. The development of $\mathcal{C}$ provides a systematic framework for the units of continuous logic and their interaction, facilitating a rigorous examination of the category's structural properties. The structure of $\mathcal{C}$ suggests the presence of certain universal objects, whose existence has yet to be proven through logic-based methods, offering an opportunity for category-theoretic insights to influence continuous logic. The study also explores a functor that maps $\mathcal{C}$ onto the category $\mathcal{M}$ of metric spaces, showing that the addition of finite sups and the multiplication by 0 functor provides a universal solution for embedding $\mathcal{M}$ into $\mathcal{C}$. The relationship between the functors that map $\mathcal{C}$ onto $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{M}$ is examined through a comparison of their universal properties. On account of the rising intricacy of software systems, validating them thoroughly is no longer feasible in the traditional sense. Consequently, the task of testing these systems is endless, yet a practical problem arises in selecting which cases to run first. Research has provided several approaches to address this issue, but they often fall short of being usable in real-world scenarios due to impractical computation requirements or inaccurate results. In the context of validating software systems, we employ a novel algorithm that chooses test cases based on their uniqueness and coverage of code fragments, relying on singular value decomposition and a heuristic optimization technique. Given its analytical nature, this algorithm is suitable for large-scale software systems, offering a polynomial computational complexity. To improve its performance in real-time scenarios, we have modified it to parallelize its calculations, making it efficient for smaller systems as well. The modified algorithm applies parallel programming techniques, including multithreading and message passing, to reduce its computational complexity. The proposed paradigm includes two interdependent algorithms: selecting relevant code fragments and assigning scores to them for prioritization purposes. The first algorithm employs a parallel variant of the Burkhard-Kellerman algorithm, while the second relies on a parallel version of the random projection technique. The test case choice algorithm combines these results to determine which test cases to run first. The proposed algorithm has been validated by comparing it against related approaches, including using the NASA metrics toolset on seven software systems, ranging from small to extremely large in scale. The validation demonstrated that our algorithm matches or exceeds the performance of the competing approaches, showcasing its accuracy and efficiency. To ensure the reliability of our results, we have performed extensive experiments, repeating the tests multiple times and analyzing the outcomes to rule out any chance factors. The proposed algorithm has been implemented using parallel programming techniques, including OpenMP, to ensure its compatibility with diverse hardware configurations. A combination of several data sources, including text-based information from individuals in suicidal crisis and their related medical history, is used to develop a predictive model. This model aims to identify individuals who are more likely to engage in suicidal behavior. The dataset is drawn from the Suicidal Ideation dataset on Kaggle, which contains data on three classes of suicidal thoughts. We propose a novel deep sequential model that integrates the application of CNN, RNN, and GRU in a hierarchical manner to extract relevant features from the given data. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through experiments conducted on the Suicidal Ideation dataset, with our model outperforming state-of-the-art baselines established on prior research. Subsequently, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the proposed model using a qualitative case study of 10 data entries, which highlights the substantial differences in the predicted probabilities of suicidal behavior associated with each entry. The proposed model exhibits high accuracy in predicting suicidal behavior, with an AUC of 0.8977, which is significantly higher than the baseline models. Moreover, this model is capable of accurately identifying individuals at risk of suicidal behavior by analyzing their medical history and identifying critical time points that increase the likelihood of suicidal behavior. The proposed model is versatile and can be utilized in text-based medical information to predict suicidal behavior in individuals. Conventional radio map estimation approaches rely on densely spaced mobile sensor stations collecting data in parallel, which is impractical for wide-area coverage with high resolution. Our approach is adaptable to various wireless channel models and allows integrating diverse knowledge sources into the radio map estimation process. This paper outlines a novel approach, GLA, for detecting anomalies in continuous time series data by leveraging Hidden Markov Models and clustering techniques. Our method involves three primary stages: first, we use HMMs to generate likelihood scores for individual models applied to sequential windows of the data, then group these scores with others that exhibit similar behavior, and finally, identify outliers within these clusters as anomalies. Due to the computationally intensive nature of training HMMs on large datasets, we also present an optimized variation of the method, OptGLA, which incorporates several innovations to enhance its efficiency. Our proposed methods are demonstrated to be effective through extensive evaluation on synthetic and real-world time series datasets, including an example analysis of a medical condition based on patient speech patterns. Our code is freely accessible on GitHub. Our experiments show that OptGLA surpasses the performance of multiple baseline methods in anomaly detection across diverse data types, often by substantial margins, while achieving notable speedups of up to 2 orders of magnitude in some cases. Notably, in a specific use case involving medical speech data, OptGLA achieved a recall rate of 97.2%, significantly outperforming the best competing method with a recall rate of 88.5%. This research delves into a verification method that combines audio, visual, and thermal modalities to accurately identify individuals. As a more robust approach than individual modalities, this multi-modal system is explored in various verification tasks, including verification, manipulation, attribution, aggregation, and fusion. Through analysis, we demonstrate that fusion tasks are highly susceptible to mode-mixed attacks, whereas verification tasks are relatively resilient. Moreover, we show that the system's confidence in identification can be quantitatively estimated. To this end, we introduce novel metrics for evaluating multi-modal system robustness and performance, leveraging thermal images and audio-thermal modalities that complement existing visual-based systems. Moreover, we identify situations in which multi-modal verification offers advantages over visual-based approaches, such as identifying individuals in camouflage or when facial features are occluded. This work culminates in a comprehensive evaluation of deep learning-based multi-modal systems on publicly available datasets. Our findings indicate that these systems can achieve performance comparable to that of state-of-the-art visual-based methods while offering enhanced robustness against adversarial attacks and improved identification confidence estimation. Ultimately, this study seeks to contribute to the development of more effective multi-modal individual verification systems. However, determining visual compatibility is a complex task because it relies on intricate analysis of clothing items and their mutual interactions. According to a survey conducted by The Fashion Spot, a prominent online community of fashion enthusiasts, accurately predicting visual compatibility often eludes machine learning models. In this research, we present the Visual InCompatibility TransfORmer (VICTOR) – a cutting-edge solution for this complex problem. VICTOR's innovative architecture combines three distinct networks: (i) an encoder, (ii) an interaction network, and (iii) a contrastive learning network. By contrastively learning invariant features from real-world outfit images and artificially assembled item sets, VICTOR surpasses the state-of-the-art performance on the FashionISTA dataset, attaining an accuracy of 62.76%, 3.8% and 8.6% higher than the existing best methods, the human evaluation results, and the random guess, respectively. Moreover, we create Visual Item Network (VIN), an auxiliary graph convolutional network that complements VICTOR's design to leverage the inherent structure of fashion items and their visual relationships in a large scale. VIN applies a structural embedding technique to merge individual clothing items into visually compatible outfits, preserving their inherent structure along the way. By applying VIN to real-world data, we observe a substantial decrease (8.6% to 10.3%), and in some cases an improvement (5.2% to 6.1%), in the accuracy of visual compatibility predictions when compared to models that disregard this structural information. This research involves analyzing gravity waves in the Martian thermosphere by examining density observations from the Mars Global Surveyor, Odyssey, Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, and Mars Atmosphere and Volatile Evolution missions. The findings reveal a wide range of gravity waves present in the Martian upper atmosphere, with the majority occurring at mid-latitude and significantly affecting the transition region between the thermosphere and exosphere. These gravity waves spread to the polar regions during the Martian polar winter, causing an increase of up to 110% in the scale height at the high latitudes, and lead to the accumulation of energy and particles at the polar mesosphere, which may influence the formation of the Martian polar jets. This research also identifies gravity waves in the atmospheric extension layer, where they become largely horizontal and largely weaken as they ascend to the exosphere, but where a persistent structure made up of multiple consecutive nodes and antinodes still exists at a distance of around 338 km from the Martian ground level. The objective of this research is to control sound generation through image input, leveraging unsupervised learning techniques to expand the repertoire of controllable visual cues and explore multisensory integration mechanisms. To achieve this, we develop a unsupervised conditional vector variational autoencoder that learns to map visually relevant information from image input to a compact latent space. Furthermore, we demonstrate the ability of our method to create an diverse range of audiovisual content, including dynamic sounds and soundscapes, entirely autonomously. Moreover, we show that our method enables the creation of custom keywords driving sound generation using unlabeled dataset examples, thereby facilitating the generation of desired sounds upon input of corresponding keywords. To our knowledge, this research presents the first completely unsupervised approach to controlling sound generation through image input. A series of listening tests confirm the diversity of sounds generated, and our method outperforms baseline approaches in multisensory integration. To ensure fair elections, it's crucial to monitor the candidate selection process. However, when electoral boundaries are manipulated for political gain, it's challenging to detect the resulting bias. We've developed a method to quantify this bias by leveraging insights from statistical physics. From an electoral map, we've created a tool to generate a dynamic system that undergoes simulated cooling. The resulting candidate selection pattern, or its nearest stable state, accurately represents the influence of each politician. The position of each politician in this order reflects the politician's degree of influence, or "weight." This weight effectively captures the politician's advantage and can be used to measure the bias in elections. Like other metrics in statistical physics, this weight diminishes as the cooling process converges to a balanced state. We've established that this weight is a reliable indicator of bias under two established assumptions. We've also developed a metric to gauge the overall bias in elections, or "systemic bias." This bias score represents the average influence of each politician and can be calculated from individual weights. The bias score effectively captures the overall unfairness in elections. To illustrate the effectiveness of our approach, we've analyzed real-world electoral maps and simulated cooling processes. Our results confirm that this method produces a range of outcomes, or "histories," that correspond to the politicians' known degrees of influence. We've verified that the weight and system score obtained through our method align with established physical laws. Moreover, our approach is versatile and adaptable to various election scoring methods. Furthermore, we've simulated an experiment where we randomly altered the electoral maps while keeping the candidate selection order constant. Our findings confirm that the weight and system score are robust indicators of bias under different map arrangements. In conclusion, our method is a groundbreaking approach that uses statistical physics to quantify the bias in elections. By combining insights from simulated cooling, we've developed a powerful tool to measure the overall unfairness in elections and a new metric to track each politician's advantage. This work is a significant contribution to the study of electoral bias and has immense potential for applications in political science and other fields. The code for our approach is openly available on GitHub. Additionally, we've created an interactive tool that enables users to calculate the weight and system score for any electoral map. This tool allows users to upload their own electoral maps and explore the weight and system score in a range of scenarios. With this method, we can ensure fair elections by detecting and mitigating electoral bias. Similarly, this approach can be applied to other systems by modeling their dynamics and analyzing their state.

Despite widespread vaccination, a substantial number of people still harbor doubts due to misinformation disseminated on social media regarding COVID-19 vaccines. Misinformation promotes anti-vaccine sentiment, a concern that needs to be addressed through monitoring misinformation spread online. We developed a novel framework to track the spread of misinformation, pinpoint its source, and distinguish between acceptance or rejection of such misinformation within Twitter discussions. We gathered datasets for COVID-19 vaccines and specific false narratives to study users' varying responses, such as retweeting or creating new tweets, to further analyze the impact of misinformation. Our experiments yielded three significant outcomes: first, we successfully mapped the online dissemination of misinformation; second, we accurately classified users' views on misinformation with an accuracy of 95% or higher; and third, we successfully predicted a user's future reaction to new misinformation with a 93% accuracy rate. Our approach contributes to efforts monitoring the spread of misinformation and addressing concerns regarding COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy. Advancements in attosecond science hold great potential to reveal the fundamental dynamics of electronic motion within matter, contingent on achieving two interconnected technological breakthroughs linked to high-order harmonic generation sources. Firstly, achieving a higher photon flux would allow researchers to measure even the most minute processes, while also achieving a higher degree of temporal focusing would provide an enhanced intensity for a shorter duration, enabling precise analysis of electronic interactions. By utilizing a gas-filled hollow-core fiber in conjunction with a laser pulse having a broad intensity range from regulated tunable infrared oscillations to tightly condensed attosecond pulses, our research demonstrates the first instance of simultaneously achieving both a high photon flux and a highly focused pulse duration. Our simulations indicate that the temporal modulation of the driver pulse can be replicated in the attosecond pulse, enabling the exploration of coherent phenomena in hollow-core waveguides, as well as allowing for adjustable pulse duration and photon flux modulation of HGHG sources, potentially leading to significant breakthroughs in the field of attosecond science. Additionally, the observed pulse dynamics can serve as a pulse-shaping tool, allowing for the first application of spatial soliton technology to the field of attosecond science and regenerative amplification systems. Ultimately, this research may pave the way for achieving the sought-after attosecond, single-photon-nuclear resolution in scientific measurements. In achieving this goal, our research also identifies a candidate for a highly stable, high-photon-flux extreme ultraviolet laser source with a very high degree of temporal focusing, enabling it to deliver intense, single-shot pulses lasting merely 35 attoseconds. This source could potentially be incorporated into table-top setups for attosecond pulse applications, thus paving the way for a widespread dissemination of attosecond pulse technology. Our research may also lead to significant advancements in the field of superfluids, as it reveals the interaction of intense laser pulses within liquid helium at extremely low temperatures, thereby enabling researchers to control the wave dynamics within the resulting attosecond pulse. This innovative application could ultimately enable the development of a novel, room-temperature source for attosecond pulse generation. We identify two primary types of domain wall states: a high-mercury regime characterized by increased capacitance due to domain wall perturbations, and a low-mercury regime in which the capacitance decreases. The success of Deep Learning methods in image processing and other fields has created a high demand for efficient and effective neural networks capable of handling 3D data. Despite the advancements, current methods still face challenges such as complex and time-consuming data transformation processes and the limited availability of labeled data. This study aims to improve the effectiveness of Neural Networks in point cloud handling by focusing on two critical aspects: the graph convolutional module and the loss function. We introduce a groundbreaking type of Trojan attack, which can be triggered without needing the trainer to be present. In this scenario, an attacker crafts malicious models that can remain undetected during the training process, resulting in backdoored classification models. These malicious models can then be activated by a trigger, allowing the attacker to induce erroneous classifications in the inference phase. To achieve this, we utilize semantic similarity to substitute key model layers with equivalent layers from pre-trained semantic representation models. Our experiment-based evaluation confirms the efficacy of this approach and shows that existing detection methods are largely ineffective against this new attack method. Furthermore, we propose a novel boundary-based trigger generation method that can activate backdoors in both image and text classification models. Our approach offers several advantages over previous Trojan attacks, notably due to its minimal impact on model performance, lack of dependence on input triggers, and resistance to common backdoor detection techniques. We are developing an image slicer for an integral field device, ROSIE, to integrate with the IMACS spectrograph on the Magellan Baade Telescope at the Las Campanas Observatory. By splitting the 50.4 x 53.5 field of view into four subfields, and further segmenting these into 21 individual 2.7 x 5.3 slices, we'll achieve four pseudo-slits, spaced six arcminutes apart. This will allow for a spectral range of 1800 Angstroms with a resolution of 2000. Our current progress includes preparing the optics, coating the first slicer, crafting the mounts, and writing the software, all aiming to enhance IMACS's functionality by facilitating the efficient examination of expansive astronomical objects like nebulae and galaxies.

In this paper, the carbon-carbon fusion research is revisited to incorporate the latest developments. Specifically, key experimental and theoretical findings from a recent analysis by Beck {\it et al.} (Eur. Phys. J. A {\bf 56}, 97 (2020)) are considered to outline the pathway for enhancing low-energy astrophysical $S$-factor determinations via new Threshold Hand Mirror (THM) measurements. These experiments can provide a direct $S$-factor value at the energy of zero, eliminating the need for polynomial fits. This approach offers several advantages over standard analyses relying on fits. Discussion is also given to recent attempts to refine the THM analysis technique. Additionally, a comparison of experimental $S$-factor values from THM, free-borne, and targeted $K$-shell ion beam-catcher (KIB) experiments is presented to highlight their relationships. It is demonstrated that the THM and KIBK values converge at low energies, whereas those from free-borne experiments appear shifted due to non-astrophysical contributions. Finally, a weighted average of the THM and KIBK measured $S$-factor values is presented to reflect the current understanding of the $^{12}{\rm C}+{}^{12}{\rm C}$ reaction near the astrophysical energy of $E_{\rm c.m.}=4.92$ MeV, along with a discussion of its implications for stellar nucleosynthesis models. Moreover, a brief overview is given to recent and upcoming THM applications for other reactions important to astrophysics and nuclear energy. These include analyses of the $^{12}{\rm C}+{}^{16}{\rm O}$ reaction and p+p fusion. New results are also presented for the $^{16}{\rm O}+{}^{16}{\rm O}$ reaction to explore the possibility of a low-energy barrier, which could improve our understanding of the $^{12}{\rm C}$ nucleosynthesis in massive stars. This study may also provide insight into the formation of heavy elements through the explosive $^{16}{\rm O}$ nucleosynthesis in supernovae. It is further suggested that the THM analysis technique could be widely adopted for a large-scale experiment to measure the $S$-factor for the $^{12}{\rm C}$ reaction over a broad energy range, which would enable a direct comparison with the current analysis and would refine our understanding of the reaction. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become a preferred method for wireless localization based on channel state information (CSI). However, previous research using DNNs has some drawbacks. Firstly, the proposed models often rely on synthetic data for training and may not perform well with real-world data. Secondly, the channel representations used in DNNs are usually fixed, which does not leverage the diverse characteristics of CSI. Lastly, the last layer of existing DNNs usually consists of a traditional Euclidean distance-based localization module that may not fully utilize the raw CSI features. 

This paper proposes a novel deep learning approach that employs an attention mechanism in conjunction with a conventional DNN. The attention mechanism allows for dynamic feature extraction and weight assignment of the raw CSI, thereby leveraging the diverse characteristics of CSI. We also introduce a dataset with real Wi-Fi signals that can be used for training and testing DNNs. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed attention-assisted DNN (Att-DNN) achieves a significant performance improvement over the conventional DNN. Moreover, Att-DNN shows superior localization accuracy when compared to several benchmarking methods. The code and dataset are publicly available on GitHub. 

This research makes several significant contributions. Firstly, we successfully trained a DNN using real Wi-Fi signals in a large indoor space without relying on synthetic data. Secondly, we designed a dynamic channel representation approach that assigns weights to raw CSI based on the diversity of its characteristics. Thirdly, we proposed a novel Att-DNN model that outperforms the conventional DNN and several benchmarking methods. Lastly, we made available the code and dataset for this research to facilitate further study.

This paper presents a comprehensive framework for modal logic by linking different types of modal logic to the topological properties of specific categories. Building on similar relationships between topological categories and other logical systems, this relationship is fundamental and inherently axiomatic. In the first installment of a two-part series, we will establish the relationship between topological categories and modal logic based on fibrations and monomorphic fibrations, while the second part will explore closed categories and the relationship with first-order logic. This paper's main contributions are the introduction of a hierarchical system that relates different types of modal logic to each other and the development of a universal model for modal logic that makes it possible to compare and contrast various extensions of modal logic in an objective way. In particular, we will show that S5 is a singular, fundamental type of modal logic and that other extensions, such as the modal logic of provability ($PML"), is both similar to S5 and yet distinct from it in terms of the properties of the underlying modal formula space. This model also provides a comprehensive framework for reporting on the outcome of the comparison between different types of modal logic. Furthermore, this paper will introduce the concept of "modal units" as a fundamental building block for developing the logic of complex modal formulas and establish the relationship between different modal units and the type of topological structures they represent. In conjunction with the second part of the paper, this relationship will enable us to conclude that first-order modal logic is equivalent to the modal logic of provability. In addition to these key contributions, we also revisit and reinterpret well-known results in the light of this new framework, including the dualization of K4 and the duality between S5 and the set of continuous functions on the unit interval. This paper also identifies an unexpected connection between these instructional methods and the theory of flows over the unit interval. This study is an extension of our earlier research on the category-theoretic description of modal logic, in particular our research on the modal logic of provability. This research was previously reported at the Cauchy Conference and the Moscow Modevian Conference. This study is a response to the query of its reviewer as to the relationship between our research on the category-theoretic description of modal logic and the well-known research of Montaigne on the category-theoretic description of provability, as well as a follow-up to our earlier research on the comparison between different modal logic extensions using category-theoretic description. A graph's edge coloring can be described as a proper coloring of its edges, where each edge has a distinct color assigned to it. An important question in the study of graph theory is whether a given graph can be colored in a specific way depending on its structure. In this paper, we explore this idea of edge coloring on certain types of graphs, examining if a certain coloring is always possible given a graph's properties. Our research reveals a counterexample to a previously proposed conjecture about the ease of creating edge colorings on certain types of graphs. The counterexample is particularly significant as it challenges the conjecture for a specific class of graphs that are both bipartite and cubic in structure. It's worth noting that forming a bipartite graph means the graph can be divided into two separate sets of vertices with no connections within those sets. A cubic graph, on the other hand, means every vertex has exactly three connections leading out of it. The counterexample presented in this paper is specifically a bipartite cubic graph called the K_4-free bipartite cubic graph. Our research shows this graph cannot be easily colored in a specific way, directly refuting the proposed conjecture. Moreover, our study also reveals more general instances of graphs for which it is difficult to create edge colorings, expanding on previous research in the field. The entire proof of our counterexample and these more general instances is presented in this paper. One interesting finding is that examining a larger version of the graph results in it being easily colorable, which suggests there may be a key size or structure characteristic that distinguishes easily colorable and hard-to-color graphs. Finally, our research presents another useful discovery that helps distinguish easily colorable and hard-to-color graphs. In particular, we show a particular graph is easily colorable if it contains a specific structure within it, which is not present in our counterexample graph. COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but users had to rely on a local installation to utilize its full range of features. Despite being available in open-source form, accessing these features required significant technical expertise. To address this limitation, we have developed ShinyCOPASI, a web-based user interface that makes COPASI's tools easily accessible to a broader audience within a web browser. Built with R using four interdependent packages, ShinyCOPASI allows users to import, run, and analyze COPASI models through a simple and intuitive web interface. It offers a range of functional tools, including model validation, parameter estimation, equilibrium and pathway analysis, and single-trajectory simulations, among others. To ensure compatibility with the widest possible range of models, ShinyCOPASI includes a model conversion function, enabling users to upload and analyze models in multiple formats. Furthermore, our web application includes a comprehensive guide with Frequently Asked Questions to assist users who are new to COPASI or biochemistry modeling in general. ShinyCOPASI is available at http://shiny.copasi.org/ and model files can be accessed at https://github.com/copasi/ShinyCOPASI/tree/master/models. Additionally, the R code for ShinyCOPASI can be found on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/copasi/ShinyCOPASI. Please note that ShinyCOPASI requires an R and Python installation to function, but we have included pre-packaged R libraries and Python bioinformatics tools to streamline the user experience. Quantifying uncertainty in machine learning models is a burgeoning field that addresses several critical challenges. First, it resolves the long-standing issue of defining uncertainty in data. Furthermore, it bridges the gap between classical probabilistic learning and modern deep learning methods. Lastly, it enables the use of performance metrics that properly account for uncertainty, thereby ensuring fair comparison of models handling noisy or missing data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our uncertainty metrics in evaluating models by consistently outperforming existing methods in theoretical and practical scenarios, including regression, classification, computer vision, and clinical risk prediction tasks. To facilitate replicability, our implementation of the proposed methods is made available on GitHub, along with extensive example use cases that can be run using the provided code. Ultimately, this research contributes to the development of a comprehensive framework for comparing machine learning models based on their capacity to handle uncertainty. The research also highlights potential future areas of investigation in this domain. Additionally, it explores the potential applications of deep learning in fields that involve small or unusual data sets. We hypothesize that deep learning methods can successfully tackle such data sets. To support this claim, we present a series of experiments involving real-world risk prediction tasks. Our research further examines the intersection of deep learning and uncertainty in the context of small data sets. The research explores two possible approaches to embedding uncertainty in the loss function and demonstrates their efficacy through numerical examples. The results of these numerical experiments, along with the associated code, are made accessible for replicability purposes. Lastly, we propose an alternative technique for modeling binary outcomes under censored data, where the model parameters are regulated by two distinct types of information. The research is motivated by our analysis of the challenges and limitations of existing deep learning methods for survival analysis. The efficiency and accuracy of our proposed approach are validated through numerical examples, along with the provision of reproducible code. iteration loop utilizing an inexact generalized minimum residual method, specifically 
the GMRES algorithm, to solve the generalized eigenvalue problem in each PI cycle. 
By accepting an approximation, our method exceeds traditional PI in computational 
efficiency for large-scale MDPs while remaining accurate in terms of optimal policy 
recovery. We demonstrate theoretical and experimental results verifying the convergence 
of our algorithm. Furthermore, we investigate how its convergence rate relates to 
the GMRES parameters and the characteristics of the Markov process. We show through 
experiments that, in certain situations, iterative methods like GMRES can outperform 
direct solving approaches for large-scale MDPs. The code for our method is available 
on GitHub at https://github.com/melarae/IGGMRES_PI. We propose calling our iteration

We develop and implement a novel, numerically efficient approach to solve DGLAP equations using a specialized method that enables multiple PDF sets to be computed simultaneously from a single evolution, enhancing convergence for different x values. This strategy involves representing parton distribution functions as grid-based arrays and employing iterative WKB-like methods, specifically the FWK scheme, to improve convergence, which can be further enhanced by incorporating DGLAP momentum dependence. We find that using the FWK scheme, especially the enhanced version, results in faster convergence compared to other methods, and we demonstrate the feasibility of computing multiple PDF sets with high precision using this method. Furthermore, we found that using the DGLAP momentum dependence has a negligible impact on the final results but can reduce the number of iterations required to achieve a specified level of accuracy. We verified and validated our implementation through comparisons with existing PDF analyses and by computing parton distribution functions for specific scales and sets while also examining the impact of neglecting DGLAP momentum dependence on the results. Additionally, we explored how the grid size affects the accuracy of the parton distribution functions and found that using FWK scheme with four iterations and grid size three or four yields results that are in agreement with six-digit accuracy using DGLAP momentum dependence. We expect this approach to be especially useful for computing PDFs on GPUs or in FPGAs. We established a public repository that includes our implementation, along with benchmarking tools, to facilitate further comparisons and assessments. We discovered that accounting for DGLAP momentum dependence has a minor impact but improves convergence, and we estimated that employing FWK scheme reduces parton distribution computation time by a factor of approximately 1.8 compared to traditional methods. The objective of this research was to examine how these soils change at different sintering temperatures, affecting their mechanical properties and ability to be shaped and consolidated. Findings reveal that soils compacted with a pressure of 50 MPa exhibited optimal mechanical properties. The sintering temperature significantly impacted the samples' microstructures and ultimate strength. Notably, the room temperature strength of the Martian samples reached a remarkable 1.91 MPa, while the lunar samples reached 2.07 MPa. The fusion point was also reached in both types of soil, at 1255°C for Mars and 1140°C for the Moon. The reduction in porosity across all temperature conditions remained steady, averaging 3.5% less porosity for every 100°C increase. Despite similar trends in mechanical properties and microstructure, the lunar regolith developed a unique core-shell structure, while the Martian regolith had a uniformly fine-grained structure. Additionally, the room temperature strength of the lunar regolith was largely affected by its sintering temperature, while the Martian regolith's room temperature strength was more influenced by its compaction pressure. We have compiled a comprehensive dataset of 240 galaxies with consistent spectral energy distributions observed from near-infrared to ultraviolet wavelengths, and with established redshifts, to facilitate a thorough analysis of star formation rates across different time periods.  By utilizing the MAGPHYS SED fitting model, we have calculated star formation rates at various epochs, and in this study, we examine the reliability of these predictions using the bracket gamma line as a benchmark to measure star formation rates in galaxies.  To calculate the bracket gamma line, we have developed a novel approach to estimate dust temperature and optical depth using the Infrared Space Observatory and Spitzer data.  Our research reveals that past star formation rates as estimated by MAGPHYS are in agreement with those derived from the bracket gamma line, and with those derived from far-infrared luminosity, but with reduced scatter when using the bracket gamma line. This paper introduces an innovative method for generating speech duration from text, specifically focusing on a synthesis model's output. By taking into account the previous and current word durations in a sentence, the proposed approach creates a duration for each word, led by a median-based estimation procedure. A crucial aspect of this method involves adjusting each word's predicted duration to conform to a prescribed frequency distribution. A control system, similar to a predictive control technique, is used to achieve this goal. This word-duration adjustment process incorporates a sequence of first-order finite differences, utilising past time series data to refine its calculations. When the sequence reaches its final iteration, each word's duration is adjusted independently, based on a prescribed frequency distribution. To further enhance the model, the sequence of first-order finite differences is repeated, but in reverse order, with each iteration incorporating additional information from the sentence's words. Experimental results using the SPLOIN corpus reveal that this approach is flexible and adaptable, with promising outcomes when combined with other duration estimation methods. Species distribution analysis can be conducted through space-only, time-only, and integrated models that consider both space and time. However, creating a comprehensive tool to address multiple aspects of ecological research has been a challenge. To bridge this gap, we have developed the spOccupancy R package, which offers a versatile approach to fitting single- and multi-species models for occupancy, species abundance, and richness across various spatial and temporal scales. The package utilizes a latent Gaussian Markov random field to model abundance and a logit link function with multiplicative hierarchical models for presence/absence. It also incorporates unique features to handle data sets with multiple species, time-sharing species, and species abundance counts. To demonstrate the package's capabilities, we present a case study on bird species occupancy in the Western United States, along with examples for single-species, multi-species, time-sharing species, and abundance models. Additionally, we discuss the benefits and limitations of using the package to address common research questions in ecological research. Understanding the spread of epidemics within networks, such as contact graphs, reveals patterns of disease transmission. However, assuming geometrical relationships between individuals may provide a more accurate representation of the spread, akin to modeling infections within spatially organized environments. Hypergraphs capture these connections by encapsulating higher-order interactions within the inherent structure of the graphed relationships. Our research explores the transmission of epidemics within hypergraphs, examining the critical thresholds at which the disease spreads through the network. Through an inversion of the spectral graph operator, we derive a necessary and sufficient condition for the extinction of the epidemic, and subsequently, the asymptotic critical threshold as the hypergraph doubles in connectivity. Additionally, we apply this method to investigate the epidemic dynamics within two specific hypergraphs: hypercubes and complete k-partite hypergraphs. In the case of the cube, we show that a simplified approximation of the spectral limit, derived from the generalized Lubotzky-Weisfelter theorem, is asymptotically equivalent to the exact critical threshold as the dimensionality of the cube increases. For the complete k-partite hypergraph, we demonstrate that the spectral limit achieves an exact match with the asymptotic critical threshold, and further, that this value represents a generalized universality for all hypergraphs with equally distributed vertex degrees. The methodology employed in this research is expected to contribute to future investigations in the field. Recent breakthroughs in understanding 2D magnetic semiconductors, exemplified by the study of CrI$_3$, have generated significant enthusiasm due to their intriguing spin-dependent properties and their potential to revolutionize spintronics and magneto-optoelectronics. Through advanced theoretical calculations, researchers investigated the behavior of spin polarization within the prototype ferromagnetic CrI$_3$ bilayer, which has an in-plane magnetization. Their investigation reveals that this ferromagnetic bilayer exhibits a rich pattern of spin texture within its uppermost valence bands, which arises from two unique spin cants resulting from the interplay of ferromagnetic order with both chirality and electrical polarization. One type of cant is a result of layer stacking asymmetry and valence state polarization, leading to equivalent canting patterns on both layers. Conversely, the other cant is a consequence of Rashba effect, which in this ferromagnetic case generates oppositely canting components on adjacent layers within the same electronic state. Additionally, researchers formulated a set of rules governing spin polarization behavior within magnetic crystals based on their magnetic symmetry properties. Lastly, they found that applying compressive strain could effectively control the shape of spin texture within ferromagnetic CrI$_3$ bilayers by creating valence-band states with spins that can be aligned. These findings significant to understanding ferromagnetic semiconductors and their potential application in spintronic devices. \\

It's assumed that individuals experience genetic evolution through mutations at a specified rate, and new individuals inherit the genetic information of their parents in a random manner. Furthermore, areas focusing more on COVID in their local news are likely to report higher case counts. To investigate the influence of local audience dynamics, we conducted additional analyses. First, when COVID-related stories account for a larger portion of overall local news, they are more likely to be covered by smaller news outlets rather than larger ones. Second, areas where COVID is more prominently covered are more likely to have a broader audience for local news. These findings provide empirical evidence of the intricate connections between the content of local news, COVID-specific coverage, and its audience, offering a comprehensive understanding of the dynamics underlying the coverage of this global pandemic in the U.S. through an online news monitoring perspective. Specifically, boosting COVID-specific coverage can lead to increased transparency and informed public decision-making, ultimately helping to control the pandemic. Moreover, recognizing the role of the audience in shaping local news can facilitate efforts to engage citizens in news creation, thus making local news more dynamic and responsive to their needs during this critical period. Conversely, our results show that the broader audience for local news is more likely to be interested in COVID-specific stories.
