Several concepts from convex analysis find counterparts in complex geometry 
by establishing correspondences via specificity and compactness. This article 
provides a detailed overview of these correspondences along with computational 
tools necessary for applying them in convex analysis. In doing so, it bridges 
the gap between convex mathematics and complex geometry by leveraging them both. 

Specific correspondences involve projecting non-linear mappings in convex analysis 
onto corresponding linear mappings in convex geometry. Examples include 
considering the Hausdorff metric's projection on the set of strictly convex 
functions. Bilinear transformations in convex analysis have their eigenvalues 
corresponding to dilations in complex geometry. This latter correspondence 
holds for any compact set. The Cauchy-Green formula can be seen as a 
generalization of the Fourier-Mellin transform. This perspective enables 
reinterpreting the Fourier-Mellin transform as an extension of the Birkhoff 
recurrent vector field. This article also demonstrates how the Helmholtz- Poincare formula finds itself an embodiment of the Fourier-Mellin transform's 
inverse. This perspective further enables reexamining Hadamard's formula in the 
light of E. Mousa's integration method of combining the Fourier-Mellin 
transform's direct and inverse applications. Finally, this article concludes by 
reinterpreting the Kullback-Leibler distance through the lens of complex 
geometry. Specifically, it shows that this distance is an expression of the 
complex Boltzmann constant, thereby deriving it from the Riemannian volume 
metric. Consequently, this article presents new proofs for the central limit 
theorem, the law of large numbers, and the log-concavity of the relative 
entropy. These proofs rely on the topological properties of compact sets in 
complex geometry. Hadamard's formula finds itself an embodiment of the 
inverse Fourier-Mellin transform. This article also explores the connection 
between the Kakutani-Fenchel duality and the complex Boltzmann constant. 
Furthermore, it shows that the entropy of a probability measure is an expression 
of the complex logarithm. Finally, this article concludes by reexamining the 
Euler-Lagrange equation in the light of specifying the complex Laplacian.

The manual process of labeling visual data for machine learning can be extremely costly and, in some cases, impossible due to data scarcity. Despite these costs, data labeling remains a fundamental component of model training in fields such as document analysis, where perfectly accurate labels are often required. This paper presents a new approach to reduce data labeling costs by approximating accurate labels using low-cost, coarse annotations. We achieve this through a simple yet effective method of combining pre-trained vision models with confidence ensemble techniques. The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated across three diverse datasets, yielding up to a 30-fold reduction in labeling costs while maintaining nearly flawless labeling accuracy. Our proposed method outperforms traditional data labeling methods by producing labels at least 10% more accurate even when costs are significantly scaled back. 

  Detailed Experimental Analysis

Our experiments were conducted on three datasets from document analysis, each with distinct challenges: Table Detection in medical research papers, Layout Analysis in invoices, and Information Extraction in identity cards. We employed a two-stage process to reduce data labeling costs: 

1. We trained a vision model using coarse annotations, then fine-tuned it using partially complete, partially annotated data. This was done to replicate a scenario where models are trained and evaluated in a real-world setting, where labels are often incomplete.

2. We compared the accuracy of models trained with our cost-reduction approach against those with traditional data labeling methods.

  Comparison with Baseline Approaches

The two primary baseline approaches for document analysis involve using either fully annotated data or models pre-trained on uncurated sources such as Wikipedia. When using fully annotated data, models are trained in an supervised setting but may be hampered by scarcity of data. On the other hand, pre-trained models lack domain-specific knowledge and often require extensive fine-tuning.

Each network in this sequence is trained separately with the goal of optimizing the corresponding hyperparameters with limited computational resources, however this approach is inefficient and poorly aligned with the original task of the network. The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval Task 6 challenge is the subject of this paper. Our approach to identifying abusive language in tweets involved two main steps. Firstly, we used the BERT language model to create a high-performance classifier that captured complex, contextual meanings, but also relied on pre-trained features from a vocabulary-count model and a LSTM classifier for comparison. Our ultimate goal was to achieve a gold-standard correlation coefficient of 0.9 or higher with a training dataset of annotated tweets, and to outperform the challenge's baseline at least marginally. Ultimately, our team finished in second place overall in the challenge. In this paper, we explore the performance of our UM-IU@LING system in detail. Our results indicate that combining the strengths of various models can yield outstanding performance inAbrasive, Threat, Sexual and Spaming tweet classification. Additionally, the paper examines the distinctive characteristics of the UM-IU@LING system that distinguished it from other competitors in the challenge. Our analysis also reveals that using the BERT language model as a base classifier enabled our team to capture the complex, nuanced meanings inherent in aggressive tweets. Furthermore, our team enhanced the base classifier with a vocabulary-count model and an LSTM model for feature engineering, thereby demonstrating that a multi-faceted approach can yield superior performance in abusive language identification. In general, the paper showcases how different machine learning architectures can contribute complementarily to the development of a robust classifier for aggressive language, and highlights the substantial benefits of using pre-trained models like BERT in natural language processing applications. Our findings also emphasize the importance of multi-faceted feature engineering in capturing the complex, contextual meanings inherent in abusive language, and the value of human annotation in natural language learning. Finally, the paper illustrates the outstanding performance of the BERT language model in a variety of NLP applications, and our team's commitment to using this model effectively in future research. Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively employed in radiology for diagnosing and treating medical conditions. Since most CT scanners produce data affected by electronic noise, post-scanning processing is necessary to remove artificial fluctuations. Furthermore, as multi-slice CT technology advances, researchers must find new methods to tackle complex problems such as polyenergetic beam models, diverse materials, and noisy data, all of which are addressed in this study. By formulating these challenges within a non-convex variational framework influenced by Moore's stability criteria, they propose an optimization approach that outperforms existing baselines in terms of reconstruction and material separation accuracy, as evidenced by experimental results. Ultimately, this proposed framework provides a reliable foundation for future medical imaging research and applications. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/alimomani16/Poly-CT. This stability, known as Moore's stability, had previously been proven for convex problems but had not been studied in the context of non-convex problems until this work was initially presented at MICCAI 2022. This research provides a variational framework that generalizes previous work on convex problems and proves the stability of iterative processes for a new set of non-convex problems. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the scarcity of labeled data and language-specific dictionaries. To address this issue, we present a novel approach by developing a unified dataset of handwritten words from diverse languages and scripts, aiming to alleviate the data limitation problem for Low Resource Handwriting Recognition (LRHWR). The proposed dataset is called the Comprehensive Handwritten Word Dataset (CHWD) and consists of 92,962 handwritten words collected from multiple languages, including Arabic, German, English, French, Nepali, and Urdu, spanning across different scripts. To evaluate the effectiveness of our dataset, we conducted experiments on three languages, leveraging the open-source PyTorchSHR framework. Our results show that using CHWD produces a substantial enhancement in the accuracy of models trained on the given languages, with gains of 14%, 12%, and 10% for Arabic, German, and English, respectively. Furthermore, we discovered that models pre-trained on CHWD achieve higher performance when tested on other languages, indicating the benefits of our dataset in addressing the problem of LRHWR. Our code, dataset, and experiments are publicly available on our website.

A novel computational approach has been devised, combining the methods of ab initio calculations through Green's function technique and multi-particle continuum relativistic nuclear potential to study the spectra and decay behavior of dense nuclear matter and individual heavy nuclei. The newly proposed method enables the calculation of relative energies between particles and the distribution of their density, thereby facilitating a deeper understanding of nuclear interactions. The technique has been successfully applied to examine the properties of the nuclei $^{48}$Ca, $^{50}$Ca, and $^{52}$Ca. The calculations were conducted without employing any parameter adjustment and yielded Pessarako-type strengths for the nuclei considered. The study found the calculated strengths to be uniform for the $^{48}$Ca, $^{50}$Ca, and $^{52}$Ca nuclei, demonstrating the method's reliability in predicting nuclear properties. The investigation also provided novel insights into the relative energies and density distribution of nuclei, specifically the outer layer of their density distribution. The findings indicate a correlation between the isotope diplication and the depth of the two-humped density distribution. Furthermore, the study reveals that the relative energy and the density at its maximum are linked in a non-linear fashion, with the Caldecutt sum being a linear combination of the two. The study also evaluates and compares the performance of two computational methods used in the study: the TGBF and TGRBF methods. While both methods yield comparable results, the TGBF method is found to be more efficient than the TGRBF method due to the following reasons: the TGBF method is simpler in its formulation; the computational cost associated with it is lower; and the results obtained from it match well with experimental data. The study further observes that the depth of the two-humped density distribution in heavy nuclei is directly proportional to the calculated Caldecutt sum. Based on these findings, a simple empirical formula is proposed to describe the density distribution in heavy nuclei at very low energies. The study also highlights the significance of employing density distribution information in phase-space, particularly in the context of relativistic nuclear collisions. Additionally, the guide highlights the achievements of the SSH model in educating students and non-experts about key topological quantum mechanics concepts through hands-on visualization. We recommend several innovative approaches to deepen the understanding of these concepts, incorporating geometric, algebraic, and numerical methods. These techniques include drawing connections between topological delocalization and Fourier transforms, using linkings as a probe for entanglement, and applying numerical computations through the Fourier harmonic series to predict the model's behavior. Lastly, the guide concludes with a showcase of student-created conceptual visualizations using numerical data from the SSH model, highlighting their understanding of complex quantum ideas. We distributed printed materials with over 120 visualizations to reach a broader audience, exceeding our expectations for the project. We derived a two-loop amplitude formula for four graviton supermultiplets in AdS$_5$ times S$^5$ using a unique combination of Poincar\'e symmetry and cosmological constant, which was previously established by Friedman. This result is an extension of a similar formula obtained by Sen for three-point functions. To obtain the two-loop amplitude formula, we combined various components, including a bilinear form related to the Wigner function, a spinor structure similar to Paulis matrices, and a degenerate meromorphic structure. This work also involves reconstructing a conformal block formula as the inner product of a Wigner function with a specific state, which was not directly apparent from twistor strings. Furthermore, we found that the inner product involves a non-trivial square root of an elliptic theta function. Additionally, we expressed the four-gravity amplitude in terms of a hypergeometric function using a Poincar\'e symmetry argument, which confirms an earlier conjecture by Sen. We also explored an analogous formula for three-point functions in AdS$_5$ times S$^5$ as a superconformal block in a twoloop amplitude, which was expressed in terms of a Wigner function and an elliptic theta function. However, we found that direct application of twoloop vertex operators is not feasible due to the absence of a suitable factorization. Instead, we used an argument based on the dressing kernel to relate three-point functions to four-point functions, which was previously established by Friedman. Lastly, we expressed the dressing kernel in terms of a conformal block and various other objects, which involves a double integration and a meromorphic structure, as well as an argument based on the dressing action. We also showed that the dressing action can be reinterpreted using a dressing kernel, which was initially described by Friedman. Moreover, we confirmed that the dressing action can be expressed in terms of a boundary condition, which was first observed by Hausel and was later reconfirmed by Zarembo. Finally, we found that the dressing action can be related to a dressing kernel through an inverse process, which was first observed by Sen. High-performance computing on GPUs significantly benefits from using global memory to allocate user-defined objects, enabled by specialized memory allocators. These allocators, however, introduce a bottleneck due to the limited bandwidth of memory allocation, especially on modern GPUs with reduced maximum allocatable memory size. We introduce DynaSOAr, a highly efficient and scalable memory allocator for allocating objects on GPUs. DynaArSOAr maintains a dynamic memory pool with user-controllable memory fragmentation level, allowing it to efficiently handle object creations and deletions while preventing the device from running out of memory. We demonstrate the performance and efficiency of DynaSOAr through a set of numerical simulation codes and an object-based sparse matrix multiplication example, showcasing its ability to achieve up to 10 times faster execution speeds and 5 times higher memory usage efficiency compared to existing allocators. We also highlight the potential areas for further research and improvement. The code for DynaSOAr is publicly available on GitHub. The $\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2'$ symmetry, resulting from the gauging of $U(1)_X$, distinguishes between three sets of third-generation fermions and fermions with smaller Yukawa couplings. A cane tube subject to internal pressure experiences both circumferential and longitudinal stresses. To assure the structural integrity of such a structure, it's crucial to understand how the longitudinal tension affects its mechanical stability. This study investigates how prestress influences the stability of a cane tube when pressed against an external, non-yielding surface. To this end, we establish a mathematical model that describes how a tube's shape changes when it's pressed from both inside and outside. To simplify the analysis, we develop a semi-analytical model based on a slice of the tube cross-section. This approach allows us to determine the conditions under which buckling occurs and to calculate the energy associated with buckling modes. Our analysis shows that both prestressing and external pressure impact the stability in opposite ways, and that a combination of these forces can result in a more stable structure. Moreover, we find that a tube with a perfectly rigid outer surface is less stable than one with an externally flexible surrounding medium. This finding is corroborated by numerical simulations that use the finite element method. A comparative analysis of theoretical and numerical results shows that the semi-analytical model presents a reliable representation of a cane tube's mechanical behavior. This model could be useful in designing, for instance, pressure vessels or biological bodies. Additionally, it may be applied to modeling other types of structures, such as spiral chimneys or biological organs, placed in a curved environment and subjected to external pressure. This could lead to new insights into the mechanical stability of such structures. To study the effects of internal and external pressures separately, we derive two reduced problems - a problem of a tube pressed from the inside and a problem of a tube pressed from the outside - and demonstrate that their solutions can be combined effectively. Furthermore, we prove that the semi-analytical model based on a tube pressed from the inside experiences a limit of stability at a certain pressure, although this value cannot be achieved due to hard constraints on the structure's walls. This limit can be attributed to a theoretical'stability well' that also exists in the problem of a tube pressed from the outside. In various fields, ensuring decision functions maintain their optimal performance under changing conditions, even with limited knowledge of their environment, is a top priority. Our study introduces an approach for guaranteeing the performance of decision functions in situations where little is known about their operation, particularly when faced with uncertain conditionality, by translating a renowned theoretical framework into a practical method for analyzing credal Bayesian networks on a computational level. The high standards set by this theoretical framework prove challenging to achieve directly in practical applications. Therefore, we propose reducing the strict requirements of this framework, replacing complex state constraints with more manageable ones, to provide reasonable assurances about decision functions within the context of credal Bayesian networks. The simplified guarantees, derived from the reliance on semi- probabilistic evidence, yield a computationally feasible problem of semi-probabilistic inference over the probabilistic circuit representing the credal Bayesian network, facilitating the application of existing specialized solvers to produce concrete certainty and uncertainty bounds for relevant quantities of interest within the network. The approach is demonstrated through the use of concrete variants of two well-known Bayesian network applications. Although this approach does not provide the strongest guarantees possible, the theoretical framework sets an impossibly high standard for semi-probabilistic evidence, making it impractical for large real-world applications. Consequently, we anticipate this method to be practical and useful in a wide range of applications. Additionally, we anticipate this approach to be adaptable to various other models derived from Bayesian networks, as well as decision functions beyond the realm of Bayesian networks. Lastly, we acknowledge that semi-probabilistic inference solvers are still an evolving area and offer an opportunity for future improvement and advancement. Nevertheless, we utilize existing solvers in our approach, combining them with a novel efficient algorithm for deriving certainties and uncertainties within credal Bayesian networks, particularly when dealing with semi-probabilistic evidence. The resulting method provides a practical means for ensuring the performance of decision functions in applications where little is known about their operation, particularly under conditions of uncertainty, by leveraging the reliance on semi-probabilistic evidence. This approach is expected to be an essential tool for ensuring the optimal performance of decision functions in various real-world applications. Godel modal logics can be regarded as an extension of intutionistic modal logics with prelinearity. This study explores Godel modal logics in relation to non-classical structures, specifically in the framework of basic Godel algebras with two modal operators. It demonstrates that these algebras are representable through relational Godel structures, consisting of directed graphs with labelled paths, and establishes the equivalence between these algebras and such relational structures. Furthermore, this study considers various generalisations of the Godel modal logic to include fibre-based Godel logic, and examines the associated relational structures in relation to evolution graphs and oriented directed graphs with fibre-based paths. It shows that these modal logics can be modelled by a specific class of relational structures with fibre-based paths, and sets out the conditions under which these models are representable as fibre-based Godel structures. The study also delves into the associated algebraic structures with fibre-based modal operators and establishes their representability in relation to oriented directed graphs with fibre-based paths. In addition, this study extends the developed methodology to model both fibre-based Godel logic with two modal operators and intutionistic Godel logic with two modal operators. The study presents ordering-based Godel structures as a modelling framework for these extended logics and demonstrates their representability in relation to directed graphs with labelled paths, taking into account orientation and fibre. The results presented in this study are a contribution to the ongoing research into Godel modal logics as a means of applying mathematical concepts to the study of language. The research has applications in linguistics, where researchers model language using directed graphs and intutionistic modal logic, and in mathematics, where Godel modal logic with fibre-based logic has been utilised as a means of modelling non-linear structures. The research has also led to the consideration of new modal logics with fibre-based logic. The study provides a new modelling framework in the form of oriented directed graphs with fibre-based paths for these logics and examines the Godel modal logic with fibre-based logic in the context of intutionistic modal logic with fibre-based logic. The research has further led to the consideration of new modal logics with fibre-based logic. This research presents a novel technique for word alignment that leverages external bilingual data and is adaptable to any new language pair that can be accessed. Our method involves using a unsupervised alignment model to make predictions for an unseen sentence pair based on training from extensive monolingual data and a limited number of sentence pairs from a different language pair. We test this approach with three distinct language pairs - English, German, and Spanish - and show that it can be successfully applied to pairs like English-German and German-Spanish based on English-French bilingual data and extensive monolingual data in all three languages. Our experiments also reveal that this technique leads to a substantial reduction of approximately 50% in the time required to create fully aligned training datasets. We further demonstrate that it can also be applied to the challenging task of Bilingual ISO mapping by making use of bilingual names and monolingual data to establish a connection between names in different languages. This approach leads to a substantial reduction of approximately 30% in the time required to create fully aligned training datasets for Bilingual ISO mapping. We plan to make our code and dataset available. 

Keywords: Word alignment, Bilingual data, Monolingual data, Unsupervised, Bilingual ISO mapping, Names in different languages, Fully aligned datasets, Language modeling, External data, New language pairs.

We suggest an original primal-dual iterative algorithm designed to compute Nash equilibria for various applications, including nonconvex-quadratic and convex-quadratic matrix games. This method is inspired by a distorted resolvent strategy that treats the Bregman distance with a shifted parameter, thereby facilitating the analysis through the fixed-point theorem. Furthermore, we impose a condition on the game's matrix to ensure the algorithm's convergence to a unique Nash equilibrium without requiring the fourth-order derivative of the quadratic function. We also present a modified version of the algorithm to utilize the projection operator instead of the distorted resolvent, which enables the computation of equilibrium strategies with box constraints. The proposed algorithms are demonstrated with numerical examples and benchmark tests. Additionally, we apply our method to nonconvex-quadratic matrix games in various fields, such as semidefinite programming, kernelized combinatorial optimization, and deep learning. The latter application involves utilizing Nash equilibria to regularize the learning process and prevent the accumulation of certain strategies. The method's simplicity and performance make it an attractive approach for resolving nonconvex Nash equilibria in various computational problems. The associated MATLAB code for this study is available at https://github.com/Branche1/distorted-reshishkov/tree/master/distorted-reshishkov. The C++ code for Projected DistRes on the manifold of positive semidefinite matrices is available at https://github.com/Branche1/distres-matrix. A version of this study has been previously presented at the ICML 2022 conference under the title "Nash is Deep: Computing Equilibria via Neural Networks" (https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.06542). The distance between our work and the previously presented concept, along with key differences, are discussed at https://branche1.github.io/distres-2022/ distres-2022-neural-nash.rough. We carried out a high-resolution ARPES study on sodium and found that the observed enhancement of its electronic mass is slightly less than expected from almost-free electron models. This expected increase is caused by the electron's longer lifetime due to reduced scattering with nearby phonons, leading to a mass enhancement factor of $\xi = 1.3$. However, our enhanced mass is based on the measured energy spread, which is influenced by the electron's lifetime rather than thermal disorder. We also identified the scattering rate of electrons in sodium to be in line with predictions made by a model incorporating simple lattice structure. This result demonstrates that sodium's electron-phonon coupling is relatively weak. Additionally, we found that the electron's mean-free path in sodium is significantly longer than expected, suggesting the influence of effects not considered in simple models. A mean-free path of approximately $30\pm 5$ nm was measured, corresponding to a mean-free path of $20\pm 4$ nm predicted by a model incorporating simple lattice structure. Our study offers a benchmark against which to compare quasi-particle properties in other materials with similar electron-phonon coupling. Furthermore, it highlights the importance of considering electron-phonon coupling when interpreting data from deep burrows in momentum space. We also identified several other potential sources of error that could lead to inaccurate results in sodium. An alternative method for calculating the mass enhancement factor was also considered, using the observed density of states, which yielded a mass enhancement factor of approximately $1.8 \pm 0.5$. However, this method may be influenced by other factors, such as the electron's lifetime due to impurity scattering, limiting its reliability in sodium. A related study revealed that sodium's electron-phonon coupling is relatively weak, with a coupling constant of approximately $0.4 \pm 0.2$ meV. This study relied on measuring the curvature of quasi-particle energy dispersion, as well as other data. The structural information obtained from reflectivity data in the bulk revealed that sodium's electron-phonon coupling is relatively weak. The electron-phonon coupling constant was estimated to be $0.4 \pm 0.2$ meV, with a coupling length of approximately $3.5 \pm 1.5$ Angstroms. This study offers a benchmark against which to compare quasi-particle properties in other materials with similar electron-phonon coupling. Human vision recognizes motion patterns through analysis of movement changes, but how does this relate to the specific algorithms used in computer vision? Do these algorithms mirror human perception, or are they merely analogous? If so, can we utilize existing computer vision methods to mimic human perception? To answer these questions, we studied minimal human films to understand whether they offer insights into the underlying algorithms used in the visual processing of motion.

Computational models, such as deep networks, often draw inspiration from classical motion decomposition techniques, even though these methods are incompatible with the human kinesthetic cue, as observed in studies involving motion illusions and adaptation effects. In contrast, deep models prefer to parse scenes into stable objects rather than focusing on the underlying kinematic structure, which is preferred by human perception. 

We explore whether this discrepancy can be attributed to the inherent ambiguity in determining the underlying kinematic structure from object movements, or if other factors come into play. Specifically, we investigate whether deep models prefer stable objects over kinematic structures due to biases introduced during training, such as regularization and cross-entropy losses. 

To resolve this ambiguity, we draw a distinction between the observable kinematic structure and its underlying kinematic structure, which is not directly observable. We propose two new methods, called kinematic structure networks and kernel-based distillation, to improve the understanding of the underlying structure and demonstrate its computational value. Kernel-based distillation, in particular, offers a novel approach to leveraging knowledge from existing object detectors to better capture the intrinsic kinematic structure in minimal human films. Experimental results show that our methods enable the development of a more human-like model and outperform existing deep models in various kinematic structure representations. Furthermore, we successfully tested these methods in a challenging new task, where we had to determine the underlying structure of a complex system from video observations. Based on the outcomes, we believe that our methods could be valuable in various applications, such as motion planning and human-robot interaction. The code for our research is openly accessible on GitHub. 

In conclusion, we studied the disparity between human perception and deep models regarding dynamic object representations and proposed new methods to improve the understanding of the underlying kinematic structure in minimal human films. Our algorithms have computational value and may be useful in other applications, such as motion planning and human-robot interaction. The research offers a new perspective on dynamic object recognition and motion estimation and provides a computationally useful insight into the underlying structures in human films. Moreover, we successfully tested our methods in a new and challenging task, as observed in the provided video.

The eigenvalue is further extended to polyharmonic operators and we derive precise estimates for its first eigenvalue under both nonlinear Robin and Dirichlet boundary conditions. The estimates are expressed in terms of the eigenvalue of a corresponding linear Laplace operator, with the influence of nonlinearities on the boundary being quantitatively assessed. The analysis includes examples of polyhedral domains where the estimates are shown to be sharp. The study is a natural extension of the theory of first eigenvalue of polyharmonic operators with Dirichlet boundary conditions, with applications in estimating the first eigenvalue of various geometric objects. The estimates are also relevant to analyzing the boundedness of solutions to the $p$-Laplace equation with a nonlinear Robin boundary condition. The proof involves using a maximum principle and Caccidilli-Minacci's inequality. The utility of the estimates is demonstrated through several examples. The estimates are found to be precise for some special geometric shapes, but not others. The first eigenvalue of the $p$-Laplace operator with a nonlinear Robin boundary condition is shown to be larger in volume compared to the corresponding Dirichlet boundary condition. The study provides quantitative estimates of the influence of nonlinearities on the boundary in terms of the first eigenvalue of a corresponding linear Laplace operator. The first eigenvalue of the resulting nonlinear differential operator is then expressed in terms of the first eigenvalue of a corresponding linear Laplace operator. The study provides the first estimates of the influence of nonlinearities on the boundary in terms of the first eigenvalue of a corresponding linear Laplace operator. Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass various feature extraction techniques. A numerical example serves to illustrate our approach. Finally, a thorough evaluation of our study on real-world datasets reveals that our proposed understanding of GCNNs outperforms alternative approaches. The primary contribution of our research is to offer a systematic and intuitive explanation of GCNNs that also includes an analytical examination of their computational efficiency. Deep contextualized pre-trained models significantly improve dependency parsing performance in various languages. However, their excellence largely depends on the quantity and quality of training data. In this paper, we investigate a self-learning algorithm that can enhance dependency parsing in resource-constrained languages by leveraging unsupervised techniques to systematically label sentences in a corpus. Since labeling sentences with inaccurate parts of speech and dependencies worsens the parser's performance, a high-quality labeling method is crucial. We introduce two labelers using state-of-the-art pre-trained models for parts of speech and dependencies, and combine them with a metric that weighs the plausibility of annotations. We test our approach on three low-resource languages, namely Ubykh, Sumerian, and Middle Egyptian, and compare it with three leading benchmark parsers. We also evaluate the impact of labelers, labeling methods, and labeling quantities on performance. We provide further analysis on issues that may arise during labeling and propose potential solutions. We further demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in using labeled data from related languages as an additional training data strategy. We make our code and labeled corpus available for reproduction. Evaluation results show that our self-learning algorithm with the top performer can achieve an average drop of 6.68% in unlabeled sentence accuracy and 5.14% in root word positioning accuracy in Ubykh, 2.17% in unlabeled sentence accuracy and 0.84% in root word positioning accuracy in Sumerian, and 2.45% in unlabeled sentence accuracy and 0.63% in root word positioning accuracy in Middle Egyptian. Moreover, our self-learning algorithm with the worst performer can still attain a degradation of 5.90% in unlabeled sentence accuracy and 4.95% in root word positioning accuracy in Ubykh, 1.71% in unlabeled sentence accuracy and 0.63% in root word positioning accuracy in Sumerian, and 2.03% in unlabeled sentence accuracy and 0.51% in root word positioning accuracy in Middle Egyptian. These remarkable improvements substantiate the efficacy of our self-learning algorithm in improving dependency parsing in low-resource languages. Additionally, our research confirms that enhancing parts of speech tagging and dependency parsing simultaneously yields better outcomes than focusing on just one aspect of sentence structure. Furthermore, our experiments clearly illustrate that incorporating high-quality annotations significantly enhances performance when using unsupervised labeling methods. Currently, Choiceless Polynomial Time (CPT) stands out as the most promising approach to tackle decision problems within PTIME (polynomial time) complexity, having demonstrated the capability to be contained within PTIME and yet unseparated from it. A prominent application of CPT lies in solving queries on graphs, yet its scope extends further to general structures, including digraphs. Despite its versatile use, CPT's effectiveness in addressing symmetry in structures remains relatively unexplored. This work delves into a new method for incorporating symmetry into CPT queries over digraphs, which in turn reveals a fresh set of natural problems solvable via CPT, along with their PTIME reductions. Consequently, this leads to a significant discovery: all instances from the CFIP-class (complement of IP over finite sets with logarithmic indices) can be reduced to CPT via a flexible query language. This finding significantly broadens CPT's capacity to include not only decision problems but also counting ones. Moreover, this research presents an alternative CPT-based solution to van Engelen and Wilke's problem (equivalent to a logarithmic distance measure in digraphs), which indicates that the measure can be expressed within a specific class of first-order logic if it reaches a threshold of 2^n and provides a linearly bounded formula for any other threshold. Finally, this work proves that the set of minor closed classes has reductions to CPT and establishes a new approach to fundamental structure properties, such as the existence of source or sink vertices in digraphs. Finally, this research presents an alternative CPT-based solution to van Engelen and Wilke's problem (a measure of exponential size in digraphs) and provides reductions to CPT for Cai-Furer-Immerman Digraphs with up to three sources. A key technical tool in this research is a new method for expressing whether a digraph has a symmetric subgraph of a certain size, which in turn relies on an innovative application of the Burdick-Thm-Wilke theorem. This approach further enables the creation of an efficient algorithm for identifying minors in digraphs and the automatic generation of logical formulas for describing supergraph or subgraph properties. Those methods have independent value and can be useful in future investigations. Lastly, this research presents an alternative CPT-based solution to van Engelen and Wilke's problem (a measure of size 2^n in digraphs). Additionally, this work proves that the set of circular minor closed classes has reductions to CPT.

Computer system configuration is a complex process that requires manual input from users, but inaccurate settings can lead to performance issues and even system crashes. A semi-automated method has been developed to simplify the process, and our study investigates an innovative approach that uses program analysis to reduce the complexity of system configuration. By applying a detailed analysis to a system's architecture, a reduced configuration space can be identified that corresponds to plausible execution paths, and this space can be utilized to optimize system parameters through a form of hypothesis testing. Furthermore, our approach allows for the specialization of system configuration to be specialized at compile-time, and our general methodology is illustrated through a proof-of-concept application based on the Linux kernel's headless configuration. Our findings reveal that the reduced configuration space can be as much as 5 orders of magnitude smaller than the entire possible configuration space, and with the aid of program analysis, some system parameters can be optimized with little to no further running-time experimentation. However, our approach is not suitable for all system components, and our future work will focus on developing more precise methods for identifying and optimizing the best-fitting parameters for all system elements. Additionally, we intend to apply these findings to other domains and explore the scalability of our approach to other complex systems. This paper explores the dynamic behavior of a two-level atom interacting with a quantized electromagnetic field in a cavity. Unlike the standard Jaynes-Cummings model, which describes a cavity field evolving from vacuum to a fixed number state, our study investigates a scenario where the atom and cavity field transition from a specified non-vacuum state to the vacuum. We derive analytical solutions for the system's state, which allows us to examine key characteristics such as Rabi oscillations, entanglement transmission, and transmission rates. Notably, our results reveal the presence of dark states and anti-entanglement transmission (i.e., the reduction of entanglement between the atom and cavity field as the atom decodes information from the cavity field). Additionally, we demonstrate that in the case of weak atom-cavity coupling, the transmission rates can be quantified using the scattering theory. Furthermore, our work shows that in the weak coupling regime, the entanglement transmission is more susceptible to cavity decay than the Rabi oscillations. We also derived the conditions necessary for nearly complete transmission of entanglement, as well as the emergence of anti-entanglement transmission. Our findings could contribute to the development of novel quantum information technologies. Furthermore, our study may facilitate a deeper understanding of the interaction between a two-level atom and the quantized electromagnetic field, which is a fundamental problem in quantum electrodynamics. This work can also be generalized to study the interaction between a qubit and bosonic modes in a specific non-Jaynes-Cummings framework. Lastly, our study follows the guidelines outlined in the quantum information-to-reality roadmap. We analyze the active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle (AOUP) using a systematic method based on the Wyld expansion to examine the particle's noise, friction, and propulsion forces across a wide range of parameters. By integrating the AOUP's nonlinear dynamics into a simplified description, we gain a deeper understanding of the particle's behavior in complex environments and develop simplified models to analyze its responses under varying environmental conditions. This approach enables us, for the first time, to accurately predict the particle's long-term overall propulsion and energy expenditure in complex situations. Our results in one dimension show that its average energy expenditure is proportional to its propulsion and frictional rates, with the proportionality constant depending on its thermal noise strength. Moreover, we found that its work variations follow a nonlinear pattern in two different stages: initially, the particle's overall work is proportional to time, while in the late stage, it becomes proportional to time squared, with the constant of proportionality being time-dependent. Our analysis in two dimensions yields similar results, with the addition of pre-exponential constants that also change over time. Our research demonstrates that integrating the AOUP into a simplified description facilitates a broader understanding of the particle's behavior in complex environments. Additionally, we observed that the particle exhibits goal-directed motion only in certain regimes, with its work variations displaying non-Gaussian statistics that are asymmetric. Our study provides a new framework for analyzing active particles with memory and their responses in complex environments. This framework can be applied to analyze the behavior of active particles with memory in a wider range of situations, potentially including their collective behavior and that of their extended models. Capturing diverse movements of the human body through multiple viewpoints is a complex task.  To overcome this challenge, we have developed a large, comprehensive dataset called HUMBI, which features various poses and movements of the human body from multiple angles.  Throughout the course of a year, our team captured high-resolution video footage of 524 individuals performing 312 unique gestures in 22 different environments.  By incorporating advanced techniques to reconstruct and track 3D movements, our dataset reflects the diversity of human body movements observed in daily life.  To facilitate precise evaluation of methods for processing multiview data, we have designed a set of rigorous benchmarks that mimic real-world scenarios.  Our benchmark includes tasks such as aligning and consolidating multiple videos of the same gesture.  To further enable comprehensive evaluation, we have also developed a suite of additional challenges.  Our dataset, along with the associated benchmarks, can be accessed through our website at https://humbi-data.org.  We have established a competition where researchers can participate to solve these challenges, with the website providing full details of the competition.  Through this effort, we hope to drive progress in the field of multiview gesture recognition.  To date, state-of-the-art methods have achieved an average error rate of 14.7% in reconstructing 3D movements, which we have found to be 5.3% less accurate than human evaluation.  Our team anticipates that future advances in machine learning, with the aid of large-scale training datasets such as ours, will significantly improve the accuracy of reconstructing 3D movements.  We have estimated the potential error reduction to be as much as 40.5% if we were able to train algorithms using our dataset.  Our work has applied 2D and 3D computer vision, multiview learning, and sensorimotor skill representation techniques to develop this comprehensive dataset.  Through our research, we have identified areas of existing work that we believe to be suboptimal and have proposed new approaches to improve them. Despite the growing need for models in non-English languages, natural language processing models often face a significant limitation in their applicability to languages with limited resources. A novel approach has been developed to facilitate universal language transfer by defining a task representation format that can effectively enable model extrapolation to unfamiliar languages. This approach relies on the intrinsic characteristics of tasks and can be adopted by any existing language model, provided it's trained in a high-resource language. Through the implementation of task representations, it becomes possible to achieve model extrapolation in languages with limited resources without necessitating labels in the target language. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach yields state-of-the-art performance on BERT and RoBERTa models across six diverse NLP tasks and multiple language pairs. The code for this research is openly accessible on GitHub. The findings of this study offer a range of benefits, including enhanced resource efficiency, broader applicability, and increased robustness in model performance. Additionally, the task representation format shows potential in enabling models to handle multiple tasks and languages simultaneously, thereby paving the way for more sophisticated and adaptable models in the future. In particular, it is envisioned that this approach may contribute to applications in low-resource languages, language change detection, and styles transfer. The task representations format can also be utilized to improve model extrapolation in scenarios involving gradual decreases in data availability, thereby enhancing model robustness. The findings of this study also suggest that task representations may be employed to improve model generalizability through the incorporation of auxiliary tasks. The study provides a range of comprehensive ablation studies and examines the influence of various design elements on the quality of task representations. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that task representations can be effectively utilized to guide task selection in cases where multiple tasks compete for a shared pool of labels. The study offers a range of open connections that could be exploited for enhancing the quality of task representations, including the application of supervised and unsupervised methods, the utilization of multilingual datasets, and the incorporation of knowledge bases. Through its contributions, the study seeks to promote research in the area of natural language processing that focuses on understanding tasks through symbolic representations, thereby facilitating extrapolation, generalization, and other related applications. The study also seeks to facilitate the adoption of task representations in a wide range of language models, thereby enabling researchers to build more efficient, adaptable, and generalizable models. A recent video super-resolution approach called BasicVSR achieved top-notch results among its counterparts by using a simple yet effective teacher-student learning framework. This framework combined propeller-like information propagation with optical flow-based feature alignment to gather spatially distinct information. However, the original method had its limitations in handling motion patterns and the incorporation of teacher-student learning. To overcome these shortcomings, a refined approach called BasicVSR++ has been developed, featuring a more effective teacher model with aligned propagation and a revised student model with improved alignment mechanisms. The teacher model utilizes more efficient 3D corral propagation and asynchronized synchronous alignment to facilitate the learning process. Conversely, the revised student model utilizes alternative alignment mechanisms such as PFT and CFA in addition to reducing the parameter count of its counterpart. Experimental analysis of BasicVSR++ reveals its ability to produce superior results, particularly at intermediate scales, when compared to its predecessor and other leading video super-resolution approaches. This refinement further solidifies the reliability of teacher-student learning in the field of video super-resolution. The proposed model achieved top-notch performance in various benchmark tests and demonstrated efficient computational complexity, making it a suitable choice for practical use. The code for this model is available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/IngeMinho/BasicVSR++.yv3.0.0.0.0.0.py. It has been successfully used in the validation phase. The results of our research have been uploaded to the ECCV conference website. When employing teacher-student learning with aligned propagation, it is crucial to select appropriate alignment mechanisms to achieve the best possible results. To address this challenge, different alignment mechanisms including PFA, CFA, PFT, and CFT have been evaluated and compared to determine their relative effectiveness. The integration of BasicVSR++ into the test pipeline demonstrated its ability to produce superior results, particularly at intermediate scales, when compared to its predecessor and other leading video super-resolution approaches. The intermediate scale is where the majority of visible videos reside. The use of BasicVSR++ resulted in a significant improvement in the PSNR and SSIM metrics at this scale, outperforming its predecessor and other leading video super-resolution approaches. Furthermore, the computational complexity of BasicVRS+ was evaluated and demonstrated to be much lower than its predecessor and other leading video super-resolution approaches, making it a highly efficient model. The efficiency of BasicVRS+ was confirmed through the analysis of its parameter count and FLOPs count, revealing its superior performance in this regard.

We define new families of parametrized piecewise affine transformations on 2D and 3D spaces as generalized versions of the heterochaos baker map, initially developed as simplified models for unstable chaotic dynamics in finite dimension. Our analysis reveals that the most complex of these maps achieves a previously documented state of maximal entropy in 2D, 3D, and 4D spaces. Through numerical and analytical investigations, we identify that the entropy accessibility in 2D, 3D, and 4D spaces can be fully understood by referring to sequences of weakly mixing numbers, established for the Dyck system. Furthermore, our study illuminates the inherent dynamics of the Dyck system, and demonstrates that its numerical generation is not merely an artificial construct. By examining the ergodicity and mixing properties of the most complex generalized baker map, we establish that it is ergodically mixing but not uniformly ergodically mixing for certain parameter values in higher dimensions. Additionally, we show that its entropy distribution exhibits unique behavior near certain fractal sets in its attractor. Our study also evaluates the statistical convergence of approximating entropy measures generated by iteratively applying the generalized baker map. We establish that this convergence is not uniform, and that it can be achieved without generating all possible entropy measures as entropy accessibility is approached. Instead, we show that consecutive iterations of the map suffice to reach this goal within a specified error margin. Lastly, we demonstrate that the entropy distribution exhibited by the most complex generalized baker map is distinct from that of any chaotic saddle resulting from its 2D embedding, including one famously associated with the 3D standard map. Our analysis also sheds light on the ergodicity and mixing properties of its 1D uniform distribution, and establishes that its 2D ergodic product is not only maximally entropic but also accessible in all dimensions up to a certain entropy level. We also discuss how its 3D ergodic product can be achieved through an ergodic transformation in 3D space, and establish that its 4D ergodic product is only accessible through an ergodic transformation in 4D space. This paper introduces a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch-controlling capability of WaveNet. To achieve this, QPNet incorporates pitch-dependent expanded convolutional neural networks into the WaveNet structure. As a result, QPNet scales up input features by a factor of C in each depth, allowing it to capture quasi-periodic patterns in raw audio signals. Given that WaveNet struggles to model long-term patterns due to its narrow context window, QPNet incorporates a stack of WaveNet models with expanding context sizes. Additionally, a context selection mechanism similar to AttenWaveNet is integrated into each network. Experiments demonstrate that QPNet surpasses WaveNet and AttenWaveNet in terms of mean opinion score and objective measures. Moreover, the model shows promising applications in speech synthesis. Notably, Wavenet is widely employed in state-of-the-art commercial speech synthesis systems, indicating a high potential for this model to be utilized in speech synthesis systems as well as other audio generation applications. The vast majority of existing recommender systems are plagued by the limitations of profusion, sparse data, and subjective user preferences, which can be addressed through a innovative approach called SCoNI. SCoNI utilizes an advanced biclustering technique to develop personalized recommendations for users by combining two key methods: user similarity analysis and preference enrichment. By combining these two methods, SCoNI is able to create personalized recommendations, while also addressing the challenges of local, sparse and subjective user preferences. Experimental results achieved a 9.2% improvement in the accuracy of recommended lists, as well as a 30.6% improvement in coverage and a 27.6% improvement in diversity. Furthermore, SCoNI outperformed other state-of-the-art recommendation systems in a real-world test, resulting in a 6.3% improvement in user satisfaction. Through this innovation, SCoNI is able to provide more accurate and personalized recommendations to users. A public demonstration of SCoNI is available at https://tinyurl.com/SCoNI2022. The code for SCoNI is also openly accessible on GitHub at https://tinyurl.com/SCoNIcode. At the time of submission, the benchmark dataset can be downloaded from https://tinyurl.com/SCoNIdata. SCoNI combines two advanced biclustering methods to provide user-specific recommendations by leveraging user similarity analysis and preference enrichment. 
A crucial component of SCoNI is its reliance on biclusters, which are groups of users sharing similar preferences for items, and items that receive similar ratings from those users. 
Within these biclusters, users receive recommendations for the top-rated items in their shared preferences. 
Outside of their shared preferences, users are recommended the items their similar users prefer. 
By combining these two strategies, SCoNI is able to provide more accurate and personalized recommendations to users. 
Its innovation has led to a 6.3% improvement in user satisfaction in a real-world test.

However, there were still small changes left over. To understand these remaining changes, we looked at the oscillations in the sun, and found that variations in the movement of the oscillations could explain almost all of the small changes in the spectra. Different imaging applications require various color models, and sometimes it's necessary to convert between them.  Due to an missing piece in existing color models, conventional methods cannot perfectly translate style between two images when the hue component is involved.  A new approach, called NDFM, is introduced in this research to bridge this gap by modeling the forward and reverse effects of hue in a unified framework.  To achieve this, two key steps are taken:  first, a neural network is trained to capture the style of an image by condensing its colors into neighborhoods, and second, the style is reconstructed from these condensed components.  Once this network is trained, it can be used to create a conversion map that allows for style transfer between two images.  This conversion map consists of three components, and it maintains that a given target pixel's color value is determined by the color values of neighboring pixels.  This neighborhood-style representation is the core of the network's ability to translate style between image pairs.  Additionally, to ensure the conversion process preserves the given image's structure, a loss function is applied to keep the coordinate information intact.  This simple yet effective approach enables accurate color conversions between widely used image types, and it outperforms current methods in a comparison study. To efficiently handle multi-step reasoning, we propose a novel architecture consisting of a key memory network and a response memory network, connected by cross-attentional mechanisms. The key memory network compresses input videos into compact vectors, while the response memory network generates output vectors. By allowing for the cross-pollination of information between these networks, the dependent reasoning process is facilitated. In addition, we apply meta-learning to pretrain our model using a large dataset, prior to contest evaluations. Our proposed method achieved top rankings in 7 out of 11 test scenarios across three diverse datasets. Additionally, it is suggested that as snowflakes traverse these flows, selective sweeping occurs, where certain types of snowflakes are directed along specific paths, leading to the formation of distinct size-segregated layers within the snow. This paper outlines a novel probabilistic framework designed to identify the most effective treatments for individuals with colon cancer, taking into account their unique immune response. A dynamic model, drawing upon Fokker-Planck principles, is introduced to capture the dynamic interplay between the tumor and the individual's immune system. A stochastic process is applied to model the tumor's growth, incorporating random factors that can be statistically linked. Monte Carlo simulation methods are utilized to derive optimized treatment strategies, with simulated annealing and other heuristic techniques playing a crucial role in this process. A case study is presented to illustrate the application of this framework in identifying optimal treatments for individuals with colon cancer. A comprehensive list of references is included at the end of this abstract for further reading.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves assessing features of cellular and tissue alterations to determine malignancy potential. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved histopathological analysis; however, training effective models requires large, high-quality datasets that are often hard to obtain. In this study, a comprehensive dataset labeled UniToPatho was developed to support the automatic classification of colorectal adenomas and identification of abnormal tissue patterns. The dataset consists of 3,052 whole-mountainide histological images obtained from 216 resected polyps examined by multiple histopathologists. By combining these images into a single scan, we ensured that each polyp was analyzed through multiple features, mimicking the approach of human histopathologists. To simulate real clinical settings, we also identified regions of interest in H&E stained slides to exclude invasive carcinoma-related features. The adenoma classification problem was treated as a multi-class classification task, while evaluating tissue abnormalities involved comparing image regions to reference samples. Our findings show that, using a pre-trained Patch-Based Convolutional Neural Network model, we achieved near-perfect identification of abnormal tissue patterns and accurate classification of adenomas with high malignancy potential. These outcomes support the use of UniToPatho in training a machine learning model to automatically analyze histopathological images, ultimately facilitating rapid and precise characterization of colorectal polyps. The dataset is open-source, and the digital images are available on Spatio at https://spatiochallenge2021.challengeplatform.com/. Additionally, the dataset can be accessed through the UniToPatho repository at https://github.com/unitoPatho/UnitoPatho.git. Deep learning-based methods have shown efficiency in remote sensing image enhancement, but their success relies heavily on image preprocessing which often leads to compromised results. Recent innovations in generative prior techniques have improved resolution and quality by leveraging synthetic data generated by deep neural networks. However, the application of these methods to Speckle-Aided Radar Images has been limited by the necessity of noise introduction after generation. This paper presents MrSARP, a deep generative prior model that uses a hierarchical approach to produce speckle noise relevant to real ComRad images. It generates reference images at two resolution levels to facilitate detail preservation during image enhancement. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that MrSARP-generated speckle noise outperforms existing alternatives in accuracy and fidelity. Additionally, the model exhibits superior performance in image enhancement when compared to conventional and state-of-the-art methods, as evidenced by the NIQE, PSNR, and SSIM metrics. The open-source code for MrSARP can be accessed at https://github.com/tjdcatac/MrSARP.

A quantum approximate optimization algorithm variant employs a variational hybrid approach to generate approximate solutions for combinatorial optimization problems. We investigate tuning parameters in QAOA, which suffers from a high dimensionality of search space, by implementing a Bayesian approach to leverage analytical properties derived from the quantum fidelity matrix's eigenvalue problem. This tuning framework yields precise conditions and a systematically obtainable criterion to achieve critical points. Moreover, the method allows for the estimation of posterior distributions, which aids in characterizing uncertainty in approximate solution quality. Our theoretical findings are substantiated by experimental results obtained from simulating QAOA applications on quantum computers and classical hardware. We observed that the Bayesian technique produces reliable estimates of solution quality, and consequently, it facilitates the generation of accurate approximate solutions. Furthermore, the approach was found to enhance QAOA performance in various test cases. We openly provide the implementation of this tuning method in Qiskit and PySCF. Additionally, the source code containing numerical results can be accessed from our GitHub repository, and the HTML document containing the complete results can be accessed through the link provided. We anticipate that the presented research will contribute to the advancement of QAOA and promote the application of Bayesian tuning in future studies. We wish to extend our research to investigate how the presented concepts can be generalized to study the behavior of variational quantum algorithms in the thermodynamic limit. We hope that our findings will motivate the development of new methods to efficiently tune and operate these algorithms at a large scale. By adapting Sarid et al.'s work on q-learning theoretical framework, we address a key challenge that arises from relaxing the assumption that state transitions occur at discrete time intervals. Notably, we formalize the concept of continuous state transitions and present a novel algorithm, named cq-learning, along with its theoretical proof of convergence in the context of both finite and infinite state spaces. Furthermore, we showcase the practical effectiveness of our proposed method by applying it to a real-world use case - modeling pilot workload in an autonomous system. The developed algorithm succeeds in learning pilot strategies that maximize a predefined objective function, thereby enabling a systematic exploration of pilot actions and their subsequent assignment to other tasks. The presented work opens up further research opportunities in the exploration of continuous durations. Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility and metallic streak artifacts in CT scans) make this task quite challenging. To address these difficulties, this paper presents an innovative and efficient approach to localization and identification of vertebrae, which, to the best of our knowledge, outperforms all other state-of-the-art methods. Our approach, which is fully automated and tested on two large public datasets (LITS and Spine), consistently outperforms manual expert annotations, achieving an average Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.965, 0.962, and 0.953 for LITS, Spine, and combined datasets, respectively. Moreover, it significantly reduces processing time, minimizing computational costs associated with specialized hardware. Furthermore, we introduce an original evaluation metric to assess segmentation quality in 3D medical imaging, which is based on anatomical structure similarity. This proposed approach is rooted in expertise from radiology and is influenced by the inherent anatomical relationships of the spine. It encompasses vertebrae rectification to standardize anatomical variations, as well as multi-body segment identification through anatomically-constrained 3D optimization. Our optimization strategy, which is grounded in classical multi-body kinematics, ensures accurate and robust localization and identification of vertebrae in the presence of noisy CT scans. To validate the reliability of our approach, we compare the predicted vertebrae centers of mass (COM) with expert radiology targets and assess the average 3D distance between them. Additionally, we present a novel evaluation metric to assess segmentation quality in 3D medical imaging, which is based on anatomical structure similarity. Based on these results, we demonstrate that our approach is reliable at various vertebral positions and is suitable for use in radiological expert review and other applications. Our study focuses on quantum field theories that exhibit a non-trivial pattern of unitary unitarian unitarity breakdown in their BPS states, both in two and three dimensions. We develop an analytical framework to examine relative quantum geometry between two quantum field theories, utilizing spectral data that encapsulates properties of operators in both theories. We apply this framework to 2D theories undergoing Seifert transformation and 3D theories undergoing Hirzebruch genomic transformation, all while maintaining relative quantum geometry consistency. Interestingly, our results show that relative quantum geometry can reveal novel aspects of quantum field theories, potentially including non-trivial relative holonomy operators and novel relative geometric observables. Moreover, relative quantum geometry may provide a means to apply relative metrics in the analysis of quantum field theories, thus connecting relative quantum geometry to concepts in black hole physics and the moduli space of classical gravity solutions. Finally, our study brings attention to promising research paths, specifically involving the in-depth examination of unitary unitarian unitarity breakdown patterns in two and three dimensional quantum field theories as well as the development of non-linear relative metric theories, both areas deserving further investigation.

A novel physical phenomenon has been observed in which high-frequency acoustic waves completely traverse thin air gaps between multiple ceramic crystals. This occurs due to the significant attraction between the ceramic surfaces over short distances, which significantly distorts the acoustic signals at these short distances. A detailed theoretical model has been developed to explain how this phenomenon works, taking into account the interaction between surface forces and the dynamics of the acoustic signals, and it accurately predicts the conditions under which complete transmission occurs. Experiments have also been conducted to verify the model's predictions, and a method to utilize this phenomenon for force measurement at very short distances has been proposed. This method could offer a way to measure interatomic forces in the future. Additionally, this study's findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex behavior of acoustic signals in narrow air gaps and may lead to the development of more efficient surface acoustic wave devices in the future. This device could potentially improve the performance of devices such as sensors, transducers, and filters. Finally, this study’s observations may spark research into the acoustic properties of materials at the nanoscale in the future. This could lead to significant breakthroughs in nanotechnology development.

Daany is an open-source, cross-platform C# library focused on data analysis and visualization. Designed to leverage.NET Standard 2.0, this tool facilitates data manipulation, calculation, and graphical representation of data sets, in addition to performing mathematical operations on matrix and vector data. Developed atop.NET Core with maintainability and extensibility in mind, Daany is composed of twelve modular components, each addressing a distinct analytical challenge. This paper introduces Daany, outlining its underlying architecture and guiding readers through installation and configuration. A comprehensive examination of Daany's capabilities is presented, followed by a detailed analysis of its data visualization component. A concise overview of Daany's development history and future development objectives are also provided. Finally, the paper concludes with a comparison of Daany to popular data analytics libraries.

My core argument in this study is that historical accounts of the scientific revolution, which credit Galileo for establishing science as a mathematically grounded discipline, are grounded in false assumptions. This notion originated from a misleading interpretation of a 16th-century incident in which Galileo was involved. This incident, which is often cited as a milestone in the history of science, actually involved Galileo delivering a lecture in which he critiqued a certain Aristotelian geography and proposed a mathematical alternative. What's often overlooked in retelling this story is that Galileo did not in fact use his famous method to critique geometry in favor of experimentation, but rather drew his conclusions about the incompatibility of geometry with Aristotelian geography from the views of another, much earlier mathematician. This study seeks to set the record straight on this tale, but also uses it as a starting point for a broader exploration of the complex relationships between mathematics, science, and philosophy in 16th- and 17th-century Europe. In particular, I examine how certain intellectual trends emerged in 16th-century mathematical texts, but were later dropped in favor of a more demonstrative style, before eventually reemerging in the 17th century as a key component of the new scientific methodology. This recovery is illustrated through an analysis of several texts, including a previously unpublished work by Galileo, in which he explores the relationships between mathematics, science, and philosophy. Ultimately, I conclude that the scientific revolution was shaped by a diverse range of intellectual currents, but also argue that the influence of mathematics was often hidden or non-dominant, particularly in comparison to other disciplines. This paper introduces Amanuensis, an interactive system training C and Java programmers, focusing on basics such as data types, control flow, and functions. By leveraging a training method based on policy-guided reinforcement learning, Amanuensis enables seamless integration of educational content created by humans with its advanced machine learning capabilities. Unlike existing intelligent tutoring systems, which primarily utilize model learning, Amanuensis' training method allows for more efficient adaptation of learned content to new programmers, facilitating a wider range of educational topics. Additionally, Amanuensis' architecture has been demonstrated to significantly improve the performance of state-of-the-art machine learning models, such as Transformer and BERT, through a comparative study involving 18 IQ measures. To date, Amanuensis has been applied in two practical scenarios: providing beginner C programmers with a interactive guide and helping advanced Java programmers improve their coding skills using educational challenges.
